+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The world didn’t end with a bang, or even a whimper. It ended with a prolonged, bureaucratic sigh and the collective realization that nobody actually knew how to make a microchip, only how to order one. Midas adjusted the strap of his backpack, which smelled of damp canvas and the specific, sharp tang of regret. He squinted at the brick wall of the former *Kwik-E-Mart*, now the western bulwark of the settlement of ‘New Prospect’ (population: 43, one goat, and a deeply suspicious cat). "Right then," Midas said to the air at knee-height. "The graffiti says 'Sanctuary Lies Beneath The Sleeping Giant.' That’s unambiguous, isn't it?" A voice, synthesized from a voice box that had once offered three phrases—*‘Eucalyptus Yum!’*, *‘Hug Me!’*, and *‘I’m Sleepy!’*—now rasped with the static of a decade of jury-rigged firmware updates. "Ambiguity is the only currency that holds value, Midas. That, and .308 rounds. You have neither." Chewy sat propped against a rusted shopping trolley, one button eye missing, replaced by a shard of green bottle glass that gave him a permanent, rakish squint. His faux-fur was matted with dust, engine oil, and the unidentifiable residue of the Great Mayonnaise Incident of '28. A solar panel, folded like a wing, rested on his back, trickling charge into batteries that had forgotten what 'full' felt like. "The Sleeping Giant is obviously the landfill mound," Midas insisted, tapping the cryptic scrawl with a fingernail. "Look at the arrow. It’s pointing at the hill. It’s got little stick figures looking happy. One of them has a house. A *house*, Chewy. With a roof that doesn't leak irradiated dust." "Stick figures are notoriously unreliable narrators," Chewy countered, his jaw clicking *whirr-click* as it simulated a yawn. "They lack object permanence. Also, that’s not an arrow. That’s a phallus. The Ancients worshipped them. It’s a fertility symbol. You’re planning a suicide run based on a stone-age dick joke." Midas sighed, the sound of a man who had lost this argument many times before. "It’s a supply run. We need antibiotics. The goat has a cough that sounds like a lawnmower eating gravel. And I found a map in the glove box of the Prius." "The Prius that hasn't moved since the Bush administration? The map is for a shopping mall in Connecticut, Midas. We are in what used to be Nevada. The scale is wrong. The topology is wrong. The legend says 'Here Be Dragons' and someone has corrected 'Dragons' to 'Radscorpions' in biro." "It’s a lead," Midas said, hoisting the pack. "We go to the landfill. We check the 'Sanctuary'. We avoid the Radscorpions. We come home. Simple." "Simple is a lie told by complex systems to lazy observers," Chewy said, levering himself up. His servos whined a protest, a sound like a dying cat in a blender. "Fine. But I’m driving the trolley. Your steering is 'interpretive'." *** The landfill mound—affectionately known as 'Mount Trashmore' by the three people in New Prospect who still possessed affection—loomed large. It was a geological layer cake of human hubris: strata of flip-phones, strata of single-use plastics, a thick seam of fidget spinners (the Anthropocene’s most embarrassing fossil), and a crown of solar panels that had cracked before they ever paid for themselves. The "Sanctuary" turned out to be a storm drain pipe, half-swallowed by the shifting slope, guarded by a faded spray-painted sign: *NO DUMPING - VIOLATORS WILL BE PROSECUTED BY THE LAW*. "The Law," Chewy observed, scanning the darkness with an infrared sensor that flickered blue behind his glass eye. "A mythological entity. Like the Easter Bunny, or Customer Service. I haven't seen a lawyer since the Bar Association ate each other in '24." "Well, we're not dumping," Midas said, switching on a headlamp held together by electrical tape and hope. "We're withdrawing. Big difference." They slid into the pipe. It smelled of wet concrete, rat droppings, and the distinct, sweet rot of liquefying polyester. The mission went sideways at the thirty-meter mark, which was precisely when Midas stepped on a pressure plate disguised as a flattened cereal box. *Click.* It wasn't an explosion. The Ancients had run out of high explosives years ago; they were too busy fighting over the last can of spam. It was a *mechanical* trap. A counterweight dropped somewhere in the dark, and a net—woven from high-tensile fishing line and barbed wire—dropped from the ceiling. Midas, possessing the reflexes of a sedated sloth, tried to dive forward. Chewy, possessing the mass of a dense fruitcake and the traction of a greased teflon pan, was swept up instead. The net swung them both into the main sewer pipe—a vertical drop of twenty feet into a flow of something that defied classification but definitely wasn't water. " *Whirr-click-whirr*!" Chewy shouted, which translated roughly to *‘Unhand me, you fibrous bastard,’* as his claws—sharpened spoon handles epoxied to his paws—shredded the netting. They landed with a *squelch*. Midas stood up, wiping a substance off his cheek that he prayed was mud. "Okay. New plan. We follow the flow. It has to go *out*." "Flow goes to the treatment plant," Chewy said, shaking off a mutant crayfish that had latched onto his ear. "The treatment plant is the territory of the *Clan of the Chrome Dome*. Bald, painted silver, worship the Great Algorithm. They sacrifice intruders to a server rack they think is a god. Last Tuesday they tried to upload my consciousness to a toaster. I had to bite a priest’s kneecap." "Right. Against the flow, then. Upstream." "Upstream is the Industrial Estate. Territory of the *Ferro-Vores*. They eat metal. *I* am metal-adjacent, Midas. I am a snack with a personality." Midas stared at the dark tunnel stretching both ways. "Is there a third option?" "There is always a third option," Chewy said sagely. "It’s called 'Dying'. Very popular. Low barrier to entry." Before Midas could reply, the water behind them *blooped*. A head emerged. It was hairless, pale, and wore a headset fused to its skull by decades of sweat and corrosion. It blinked milky eyes. "User detected," the head droned, voice synthesized from a throat mic. "Query: Do you have an appointment for the Sanctuary? Premium Tier subscribers receive complimentary oxygen filtration." Midas blinked. "We... we saw the graffiti. 'Sanctuary Lies Beneath'." The head—attached to a body encased in a hazmat suit stitched from heavy-duty bin bags—sighed, a sound of escaping hydraulics. "Graffiti is User-Generated Content. Not Official Policy. The Sanctuary was decommissioned in '26 due to budget cuts. The ventilation fans were repurposed for a wind turbine project that fell over. You are currently standing in Overflow Sector 7. Please swipe your Citizen Card for egress." "I don't have a Citizen Card," Midas said. "I have a library card for a library that burned down. And a koala." The bin-bag figure consulted a wrist-mounted device—a Pip-Boy knockoff held together by solder and prayer. "Koala unit... Model CK-900 'Chewy'. Firmware version... *good grief*, you're running a hacked kernel from a Smart Fridge?" " It gives me *attitude*," Chewy said, bristling. "And root access. Step aside, Meat-Sack. We need antibiotics. The goat has the rattle." "Veterinary supplies are Tier 3," the figure said. "Requires 5,000 Social Credits or a functioning kidney. Do you have a functioning kidney? The left one is preferred; the right one filters the heavy metals better." "I need my kidneys," Midas said. "They're where I keep my fear." "Then you are loitering," the figure said, raising a pipe wrench. "Loitering is a Class 4 Infraction. Penalty: Recycling." "Run?" Midas asked Chewy. "Swim," Chewy corrected. "It’s faster." They turned and fled *with* the current this time, scrambling over slick concrete, pursued by the shouts of "Unauthorized Navigation! Terms of Service Violation!" and the heavy *thwump* of the wrench hitting the tunnel wall inches from Midas’s ankle. They burst from the outflow pipe onto a concrete apron, gasping, covered in sludge that would probably give them novel cancers. They were not at the treatment plant. They were not at the Industrial Estate. They were behind the *Kwik-E-Mart*. Midas stared at the familiar rusted dumpster. He stared at the graffiti on the back wall: *SANCTUARY LIES BENEATH THE SLEEPING GIANT*. He stared at the arrow pointing down at a manhole cover bolted shut. He looked at the sun, hanging low and bloody over Mount Trashmore. "We," Midas said, his voice hollow, "have made a very large circle." "Technically," Chewy said, wringing out his tail, "a spiral. Entropy demands it. Also, look at your pocket." Midas looked. A single, foil-wrapped blister pack of broad-spectrum antibiotics was tucked into his chest pocket. He didn't remember putting it there. "Did you...?" "I have *no idea* what you're talking about," Chewy said, his voice box glitching into a passable imitation of innocence. *Whirr-click.* "My logs show a three-minute gap where I entered 'Sleep Mode: Hibernate'. Perhaps the Bin-Bag Admin dropped it. Perhaps the Universe hiccupped. Perhaps the narrative demanded a payoff for the reader. Don't look a gift horse in the mouth, Midas. Especially not post-collapse. The horses are all radioactive now." Midas clutched the pills. They were warm. "We're alive." "Debatable," Chewy said, climbing onto the shopping trolley Midas had abandoned three hours ago. "We are wet, we are poisoned, my left actuator is grinding, and you have trench foot. But we have the pills. Mission Accomplished. In the broadest, most generous definition of 'Mission', 'Accomplished', and 'We'." "Home?" Midas asked, pushing the trolley. "Home," Chewy agreed. "But Midas?" "Yeah, buddy?" "Next time we need toilet paper? We use leaves. I am not doing the Sewer Quest again. My firmware can't take the narrative strain." "Deal," Midas said, kicking a rock. "But if we see a sign saying 'Free Ammo ->', we're checking it out." "Over my dead chassis," Chewy muttered, deploying his solar wing to catch the last, sickly rays of the sun. "And even then, I'll haunt your inventory screen." They trudged back toward the gates of New Prospect, two unlikely survivors in a world that had run out of instructions, arguing about the semantics of 'Sanctuary' while the goat, sensing the antibiotics, coughed a sound suspiciously like a laugh.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, philosophical asides, and satirical observations about human nature. The author effectively creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and absurdly humorous, maintaining the requested "wry, dry" tone throughout. The characterization is particularly strong. Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose optimism consistently leads him into trouble, while Chewy serves as an excellent foil - a cynical, philosophical koala whose synthesized voice delivers some of the story's best lines. Their dynamic feels authentic and drives much of the humor. The world-building is clever and detailed, with inventive touches like the "Great Mayonnaise Incident of '28," the Clan of the Chrome Dome, and the bureaucratic survivor in the sewer. These elements feel organic to the world rather than forced, and they serve the story's themes about the absurdity of both pre- and post-collapse civilization. The plot structure follows the requested format perfectly: deliberation, mission gone sideways, return home worse for wear. The circular journey that literally brings them back to where they started is both narratively satisfying and thematically appropriate. The mysterious appearance of the antibiotics provides just enough resolution without being overly neat. The prose demonstrates genuine skill, with memorable phrases like "the world didn't end with a bang, or even a whimper. It ended with a prolonged, bureaucratic sigh" and "Simple is a lie told by complex systems to lazy observers." The dialogue crackles with wit and feels natural to each character. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Occasionally the Pratchett pastiche becomes slightly heavy-handed, and a few jokes feel forced rather than organic. Some descriptive passages, while vivid, border on being overly elaborate for the story's needs. The pacing occasionally slows during exposition-heavy sections. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they succeed in their mission but through mysterious means, and they're physically worse off but spiritually unchanged. This avoids both unearned positivity and grimdark bleakness. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door didn’t jingle; it gave a tired, asthmatic wheeze. Rhys didn’t look up from the ledger. "We close in ten minutes. And before you ask, no, we don’t have the new Colleen Hoover in stock. Yes, I’ve ordered it. No, I don’t know when the distributor will actually send it. Try the WHSmith in Aberystwyth if you’re desperate." The wet footsteps on the mat didn’t retreat. They hesitated, squelched once, then stopped by the Poetry section. "I wasn't going to ask for Colleen Hoover," a voice said. Low, honeyed, with the expensive gravel of a RADA training that had cost more than Rhys’s annual turnover. "I was going to ask for *The Mabinogion*. The Sioned Davies translation. But now I feel I should buy the Colleen Hoover just to spite you." Rhys’s pen stalled. She knew that timbre. She knew the specific cadence of a man used to microphones picking up his breath. She slowly capped her pen. "We don't have Sioned Davies either," she said, not turning. "We have the Guest translation from 1849, which reads like a Victorian vicar trying to explain sex to a turnip, and a very sticky copy of the Jones and Jones edition from the seventies. Page forty-three is glued to forty-four with what I pray is Lucozade." "Lucozade is the nectar of the gods," the voice agreed. "Especially the original glass bottle kind. The plastic bottles taste like sadness and plastic." "Spoken like a true Welshman." "Spoken like a man who once drank six bottles in an hour on a bet and hallucinated a dragon on the M4." Rhys turned. He was taller than the posters suggested. Or maybe the posters just compressed him into something two-dimensional—jawline, smoulder, the 'Devil of the Silver Screen' tagline. In the flesh, under the flickering fluorescent tube light that buzzed like a trapped wasp, he looked... tired. The leather jacket was soaked through at the shoulders, darkening the suede. Dark hair curled against his forehead, too long, un-styled. He wore a baseball cap pulled low, the peak doing a poor job of hiding the bruise-purple shadows under his eyes. He was also currently holding a copy of *Fifty Shades of Grey* by the very tips of two fingers, as if it were a dead rat. **Caelan "Call Me Cael" Vance.** The tabloids’ current darling, the industry’s current headache. Three marriages, zero scandals that stuck, and a reputation for charm so potent it was legally classified as a weapon in four countries. Rhys leaned back against the desk, crossing her arms over a cardigan that had seen three decades and two cats. "The paparazzi are parked outside the Spar, aren't they?" Caelan Vance blinked. The mask of 'charming rogue' slid into place, seamless, professional. A blinding white smile. "The Spar? Good lord, no. I’m on a literary pilgrimage. *The Mabinogion*. The ancient myths. I hear there’s a very rare first edition of *Culhwch and Olwen* hidden in a cellar somewhere near the sheep dip." "Cellar flooded in '98," Rhys said. "Took the Mabinogion, the complete works of Dylan Thomas, and my grandmother’s recipe for cawl. We only saved the cawl recipe because Mam carried it out in her teeth." The smile faltered. Just a micro-fracture at the corner of his mouth. "You’re not going to ask for a selfie?" "My camera broke in 2004. It was a disposable Kodak. I dropped it in the harbour trying to photograph a seagull stealing a chip." "You're terrible at this," he said, the charm offensive shifting gears. He put the *Fifty Shades* back on the shelf—Romance, alphabetical by author, E.L. James between Henry James and Jerome K. Jerome. He turned, leaning a hip against the Poetry shelf, crossing his ankles. The posture was studied casualness. The 'I'm just a lad' pose. "Usually, by now, the owner is offering me tea, or asking me to sign a copy of my autobiography—which I didn't write, by the way, a ghostwriter did, and he made me sound like I enjoy long walks on the beach. I hate sand. It gets everywhere. It’s gritty. It’s coarse. It’s irritating. And it gets everywhere." "Anakin Skywalker," Rhys deadpanned. "See? You *do* know me. Cultural touchstone. We’re bonding." He tilted his head, the light catching the stubble on his jaw. "I’m Caelan. Though I suppose you knew that. You have that look. The 'I know exactly who you are and I am unimpressed' look. It’s... refreshing. Terrifying. Mostly terrifying." "I'm Rhys. I own the shop. I pay the rates. I shelve the books. I do not do tea. The kettle is furred up with limescale thick enough to insulate a nuclear reactor." "I like limescale. Adds character. Minerals. Good for the bones." He took a step closer. The smell of rain and expensive cologne—sandalwood, maybe, or just 'money'—drifted over the dust motes. "So, Rhys. No tea. No autograph. No squealing. Just... silence. And a ledger. What are you writing in a ledger in 2024? Tax evasion? A manifesto? The names of people who have wronged you?" "Inventory. And yes, the manifesto. You're on page three. 'Man who drips on the Persian poetry section.'" He glanced at his wet sleeve. "Guilty. I’ll buy the Persian poetry. All of it. Dry cleaning bill on me." "You can't afford it." "Try me. I made a Netflix thriller last year. They paid me enough to buy a small island. Or a very large yacht. I bought a flat in Hampstead with a mortgage that makes my accountant weep." He shrugged, a fluid roll of one shoulder. "The money is boring. The *work* is boring. Six months in a warehouse in Budapest pretending to cry over a green screen tennis ball. The only real thing lately was the rain on the M4. And this shop. It smells like dust and vanilla." "Old paper and damp," Rhys corrected. "And the vanilla is a Yankee Candle the vicar’s wife bought me for Christmas. 'Midnight Vanilla.' It smells like a headache." "I like it," he said softly. "It smells like a secret." Rhys felt the flush creep up her neck, traitorous and hot. She gripped the edge of the desk. *Stop it. He does this. He does this to baristas, to flight attendants, to the Queen. It’s a reflex. A muscle memory.* "Secrets are £4.99 in the True Crime section," she said, her voice holding, miraculously steady. "Next to the biographies of people who faked their own deaths. You’d like that. Research for the next role?" He laughed. A real one, sudden and loud, startling the dust. "God, I hope not. Though my agent *did* suggest I 'disappear for a bit' after the *Heat* magazine spread. 'Caelan Vance: Bloated, Bored, and Single in the Cotswolds.' I wasn't bloated. I was retaining water from a curry. And I wasn't bored. I was meditating." "Meditating on a sunlounger with a lager?" "Transcendental Meditation requires hydration. The lager was... a mantra." "The paparazzi are moving," Rhys said, glancing past him to the window. The long lens of a Nikon poked out from behind a hedge opposite. "They've spotted the rental car. Silver Audi. Very subtle." Caelan didn't turn. His jaw tightened, the only tell. "Of course they have. They have trackers on the car. Probably on my passport. Maybe on my cat." "You have a cat?" "I have a cat. His name is Banquo. He hates me. He sleeps on my face. It’s a toxic relationship, but the press loves it. 'Caelan’s Familiar.' 'The Purr-fect Accessory.'" He spat the words like seeds. "I feed him organic salmon. He brings me live shrews as a thank you. I wake up with wet fur on my lips and a tail in my nostril." Rhys snorted. "Serves you right for naming a cat after a ghost." "Banquo *was* a ghost. That’s the joke. High concept. My ex-wife number two named him. She took the house, the car, and the good silver. Left me the cat. Said I needed something to love me unconditionally. The irony escaped her." "And did you? Love him unconditionally?" Caelan went still. The charm evaporated, not replaced by anger, but by something rawer. He picked at a loose thread on the cuff of his jacket. "I... I’m allergic," he said quietly. "To the salmon. No, to the dander. Severely. I take antihistamines that make me groggy. I wake up puffy. The tabs say 'Vance's Bender Face.' I spend three grand a month on HEPA filters for a flat I’m barely in. And every night, I let him sleep on the pillow next to me because..." He stopped. Swallowed. "Because the flat is silent otherwise. And I hate the silence. It’s too loud." The confession hung in the air, heavier than the damp wool smell. Rhys’s chest tightened. The manifesto burned a hole in the ledger. *Page three: Man who drips on poetry. Page four: Man who poisons himself for a cat he claims to hate because he's terrified of an empty flat.* "You're an idiot," she said. The words were harsh. The tone was not. "Consensus seems to be 'yes,'" he murmured, finally looking at her. His eyes were startlingly blue, stripped of the contact-lens sheen of the screen. "But I’m a *charming* idiot. Usually. That’s the trick, isn't it? The charm. The smile. The 'Call me Cael.' Make them like you. Make them *need* to like you. Because if they stop liking you..." He tapped his temple. "The silence gets louder." "I don't like you," Rhys said. The words dropped like a stone in a well. Caelan Vance froze. The rogue, the actor, the charm machine—it all short-circuited. He blinked, the mask cracking, genuine surprise flashing across his face. "Excuse me?" "You're wet. You're dripping on my Persian poetry. You quote Star Wars at me like it's a personality trait. You talk about your ex-wives like they're plot points in your biography. You manipulate the narrative before I've even asked a question." She stepped out from behind the desk, moving into his space. She smelled of paper glue and hand sanitizer. "You're performing. Right now. You're performing 'Vulnerable Celebrity' because 'Arrogant Celebrity' didn't land. It's exhausting. And it's insulting my intelligence." She stopped, inches from him. She had to crane her neck up. He smelled of rain and sandalwood and fear. "I don't like the performance," she whispered. "It's cheap. And you're not cheap. You're just... scared." The air left his lungs in a sharp hiss. His hands, hanging loose at his sides, curled into fists. His throat worked. "Rhys," he said. Her name sounded like a prayer, or a curse. "If you keep looking at me like that—like I’m a person instead of a poster—I’m going to do something terribly unprofessional." "Like what?" The challenge was a dare. Her heart was hammering a frantic rhythm against her ribs, a trapped bird. *Run. Kiss him. Throw a book at him. Run.* "Like stay," he breathed. "Past closing. Past the paparazzi. Past the part where I charm you into the stockroom. I want to stay in the part where you tell me I'm an idiot. It’s the most honest conversation I’ve had in five years. Since before the first Oscar nomination. Since before the first marriage." The bell above the door wheezed again. A sharp *crack* of a camera shutter from outside, muffled by the glass. *Click. Click. Click.* The spell didn't break. It hardened. Caelan didn't flinch. He didn't reach for his cap. He didn't run. He looked at Rhys, really looked, and the rogue vanished, leaving behind a man standing in a puddle of his own making, holding a threadbare dignity. "Ten minutes," Rhys said, her voice cracking. She stepped back, the distance sudden and freezing. She grabbed a towel from under the counter—threadbare, floral, smelling of fabric softener—and threw it at his chest. "Dry off. You're ruining the Hafez. And if you tell a single soul I gave you a towel, I will deny it in court. I have the manifesto as evidence." Caelan caught the towel. He pressed it to his face, hiding the smile that finally, *finally*, reached his eyes. Not the white, blinding one. A crooked, lopsided, dangerous thing. "Ten minutes," he agreed, his voice muffled by floral cotton. "I’ll take the Jones and Jones Mabinogion. Sticky pages and all. I’ll pay full price. Double. Triple." "Full price. Cash. No autograph on the title page." "Wouldn't dream of it." He lowered the towel, his hair a ruin of curls. "Though... if you change your mind about the tea. I make a decent cup. If you have a microwave. And a tolerance for instant." "I have a kettle that works on fear and prayer," Rhys said, turning back to her ledger, her fingers trembling imperceptibly on the pen. "And a mug with a chip on the handle that says 'World's Okayest Boss.' I bought it for myself." "Perfect," Caelan Vance said, settling into the wingback chair by the Poetry section, opening the sticky book with reverent hands. "I love a woman who awards herself medals." Rhys didn't look up. She wrote in the ledger: *Page five: Silver Audi. Wet actor. Sticky book. Floral towel. Dangerous.* She didn't write *charming*. She wrote *dangerous*. It was the same thing, really.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing ability with vivid characterization and engaging dialogue. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Rhys's dry, sardonic Welsh bookshop owner and Caelan's performative yet vulnerable celebrity. The Welsh setting is well-established through specific details like references to Aberystwyth, the M4, and cultural touchstones. The dialogue crackles with wit and authenticity. Rhys's opening monologue about Colleen Hoover and her deadpan responses throughout feel genuine to her character. Caelan's shifting between practiced charm and genuine vulnerability is well-executed, particularly in moments like his confession about the cat Banquo. The romantic tension builds effectively through their verbal sparring. The author skillfully shows Rhys's internal conflict - outwardly resistant but inwardly affected - without heavy-handed exposition. Caelan's fragile ego and need for validation comes through clearly in his reactions to Rhys's immunity to his charm. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought passages. Descriptions like "the expensive gravel of a RADA training" and "the smell of rain and expensive cologne—sandalwood, maybe, or just 'money'" veer toward purple prose. Some metaphors feel forced, particularly the repeated references to silence being "loud." The pacing occasionally meanders with tangential details about the bookshop's history and Caelan's career that don't advance the central dynamic. The ending, while emotionally satisfying, feels slightly rushed in its resolution - Caelan's transformation from performative to genuine happens quite quickly. The writing shows strong craft in character voice and dialogue, but could benefit from tighter editing to remove some of the more indulgent descriptive passages. The core romantic premise is well-executed within the constraints of a single scene. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in the stairwell did not merely cool; it thickened, clotting in the lungs like rendered blubber. The gas-lamps mounted in their brass sconces along the spiral descent did not flicker—they *sucked*, drawing the oxygen down into the gullet of the guildhall, feeding something hungry in the dark. Aya’s hand, pale and trembling not from cold but from the low, humming resonance of the immateria pressing against her ribs, rested on the riveted iron door at the bottom. Three blasts. The foghorn moaned from the harbor, a leviathan’s groan vibrating through the bedrock, shaking the dust from the mortar. *One. Two. Three.* The Morska’s signal for *All hands lost. Abandon ship.* Aya glanced over her shoulder. Katra’s face was a mask of professional boredom, though the knuckles of the hand gripping her spring-loaded truncheon were bloodless. Simeon, ever the scholar, was checking the charge on his aetheric disruptor—a clumsy, brass-barreled thing that smelled of ozone and desperation. He looked up, caught Aya’s eye, and offered a grimace that passed for a smile. "Quiet as a drowned cathedral," Katra murmured, her voice barely disturbing the dust. "Either the raid gutted them deeper than we thought, or—" "Or the trap is sprung," Simeon finished, adjusting his spectacles. The lenses caught the sickly yellow light. "The artifact, Aya. The Scythan Key. If the Warden has it—" "Then we take it from her cold fingers," Aya said. Her voice sounded foreign to her own ears, stripped of the Court’s honeyed lilt, hardened by salt wind and candle-smoke. She pushed the door. It didn't creak. It *sighed*, swinging inward on hydraulics hissing with whale-oil pressure. The Underhold was not a vault. It was a cathedral built for a god of industry. Vaulted ceilings vanished into gloom, ribbed with exposed copper piping and load-bearing beams scarred by decades of soot. In the center, upon a dais of black basalt, sat the artifact: a spindle of pale, translucent bone—Scythan work, old as the first harpoon—cradled in a cage of electrum and warded glass. It pulsed, a slow, sick heartbeat of stolen starlight. But the artifact was not alone. Seated in a high-backed chair of whalebone and black leather, positioned perfectly between the trio and the prize, was the Warden. Mara Vell. The Iron Matron. The woman the Bluecoats had dragged away in irons not four hours past, her face splashed across the *Gazette* under the headline *SCOURGE OF THE DOCKS FINALLY CHAINED.* She looked remarkably well for a prisoner. Her greatcoat was pristine, the brass buttons polished to a mirror shine. She wore no manacles. Instead, her hands rested on the pommel of a cane-sword, the grip carved from a narwhal tusk. Flanking her, motionless as statues cast in iron, stood two figures. Not thugs. *Hulks.* Stitched men. Their skin was grey, waxy, held together by surgical steel staples and heavy black thread. Brass ports dotted their temples, venting steam with rhythmic *chuff-chuff* sounds. Their eyes were covered by riveted copper plates. Morska muscle, elevated to nightmare. "Lady Aya," the Warden said. Her voice was a file on steel. "Or should I say *Mask-Five*? You’ve been a busy little moth, burning your wings on my candles." Aya froze. The immateria surged, a cold tide in her veins, whispering *Kill them. Tear the meat from the bone.* She clamped her jaw shut, tasting copper. *Not yet. Not here. The wards on the cage—* "Warden," Aya replied, dropping into a curtsy that was pure, poisonous aristocracy. "The papers said you were bound for the Penitent Isle. I mourned the loss of your... *particular* charm at the hanging." Mara smiled. It did not reach her eyes, which were the color of a winter sea. "The Bluecoats are remarkably suggestible when one possesses the correct ledgers. And remarkably disposable when one possesses the correct *keys*." She tapped the cane-sword against the basalt. *Clang.* A sound like a funeral bell. "Stand down, children. The game is over. The Key returns to the deep where it belongs." "Simeon," Aya whispered, not turning. "The disruptor. On my mark." "Mara," Katra spat, stepping forward, truncheon extending with a *snick* of spring-steel. "You treacherous bitch. We bled for this guild. We *drowned* for it." "And you’ll bleed for it again," Mara said softly. "Or you’ll hang. The Magistrate has a special noose for guild-rats who dabble in the Arcane. *Especially* those of noble blood." The word hung in the oily air. *Noble.* The Hulks moved. Not with speed, but with the terrible inevitability of a glacier. They didn't draw weapons; they *were* weapons. One massive, stapled hand clamped onto Katra’s wrist. The steel groaned; bone snapped with a wet *pop*. Katra didn't scream—she hissed, dropping the truncheon, pivoting to drive a knee into the thing’s groin. It didn't flinch. A backhand sent her crashing into a bank of pressure gauges, glass shattering, mercury spraying like silver blood. "Katra!" Simeon screamed. He raised the disruptor, thumb finding the activator stud. "Don't," Aya commanded, the word cracking with authority she didn't feel. He hesitated. A heartbeat. The second Hulk was on him, a piston-driven fist catching him square in the sternum. Simeon folded around the impact, the disruptor clattering away into the dark, his breath stolen. Aya stood alone. The immateria screamed in her mind, a chorus of the drowned. *Let us out. Let us feast.* Shadows lengthened unnaturally around her boots, detaching from the pipes, pooling like spilled ink. The temperature plummeted; frost feathered the brass fixtures. "Ah," Mara breathed, genuine interest lighting her face. "There it is. The family curse. The *immateria*." She rose, descending the dais steps with predatory grace. "Your mother swung for less than what you’re holding back right now, girl. I watched her dance. The rope creaked a lovely tune." Aya’s mask—a porcelain visage of a weeping mermaid, edges gilded—felt suddenly suffocating. Hot. *She knows. She has always known.* "Take it off," Mara ordered the Hulk holding Simeon in a chokehold. "Let the Magistrate see the face of his daughter. Let the *Gazette* print the truth: *Aristocrat leads Thieves' Guild. Necromancy in the Nursery.*" Rough, calloused fingers—smelling of machine oil and formaldehyde—found the silk ties at the back of Aya’s head. The porcelain cracked as it was wrenched free, the cool air kissing the sweat on her brow, her cheeks, her lips. Aya kept her chin high. Her eyes, heterochromatic—one blue as a glacier, one black as the abyss—locked onto Mara’s. "Three blasts," Aya said, her voice steady despite the hammering of her heart. "The signal. *All hands lost.* You rang the bell yourself, Warden. You called the Bluecoats on your own headquarters. Why?" Mara stopped, circling her. "Because the guild is rotting, Aya. Because you little idealists think power is a prize to be won, rather than a wound to be managed. The Scythan Key..." She gestured dismissively to the pulsing bone spindle. "It doesn't open doors. It opens *things*. Rifts. The Old Ones are knocking, and you children are playing with the latch." "I know what it does," Aa said. The shadows at her feet twitched, hungry. "I know what *you* are. You’re not the Warden. You’re the gatekeeper. And you’re terrified." Mara’s hand shot out, gripping Aya’s chin, fingers digging bruises into the jaw. "Terrified? I am the only thing standing between this city and the Abyss. And you—" She shoved Aya back toward the Hulks. "You are a liability I can no longer afford. A loose thread. A noble's daughter playing revolutionary." She signaled. The Hulks seized Aya, iron grips on her upper arms, forcing her to her knees on the cold basalt. Simeon was dragged beside her, gasping, blood bubbling at his lips. Katra was hauled up, unconscious, a ragdoll of broken ribs. "Kill them," Mara said, turning toward the artifact, the Key beginning to sing in her presence, a high, thin frequency that made the fillings in Aya’s teeth ache. "Dump them in the rendering vats. No bodies, no inquests. Clean." "Warden." The word stopped Mara halfway up the dais. She paused, one hand on the warded glass. Aya knelt in the grime, bound by meat and steel, the blood of her friends drying on her cheek. She looked up, and for the first time, she did not look like a thief, or a witch, or a daughter. She looked like the Lord of the House of Vane. "If you kill us," Aa said, her voice cutting through the artifact's keening, "you lose the only leverage you have over the Admiralty. My father, Lord Vane, First Lord of the Admiralty, *adores* his wayward daughter. He pays exorbitant ransoms. He burns fleets for slights against my honor." Mara turned slowly. The Hulks’ steam vents hissed. "Your father believes you dead, girl. A riding accident. Three years past. I checked the records before I let you in." "Then he will be *delighted* to learn he was misinformed," Aya lied smoothly, the aristocrat’s mask sliding back into place over the witch’s face. "Alive, I am a fortune in political capital. A hostage to force the Admiralty’s hand on the Docklands Bill. Dead? I am a martyr. A scandal that brings the Bluecoats down on this guild with warships, not constables. You think you can manage the Abyss, Mara? Try managing a parliamentary inquiry." She leaned forward as far as the Hulks allowed. "I am the only asset in this room with a *value* exceeding the Key. Take me to my father. Negotiate the treaty. Let the boys go—they’re just gutter-rat muscle. No one cares if they hang. But me?" She bared her teeth in a grin that held no humor. "I am the scandal that topples a ministry. *Use me.*" Silence stretched, broken only by the artifact’s scream and Simeon’s ragged wheezing. Mara studied her. The foghorn sounded again, distant, mournful. *Three blasts.* A warning. Or a farewell. "Gutter-rat muscle," Mara repeated, tasting the words. "One of them carries a disruptor prototype the University would kill for. The other knows the patrol routes of every cutter in the harbor." "Then ransom them too," Aya pressed, sweat freezing on her temple. "I’ll write the letters. In my own blood, if it pleases your aesthetic. But you need a negotiator who speaks *High Court*. You need someone who can look a Lord in the eye and lie about the weather while handing him a knife. That’s me. That’s *always* been me." Mara smiled then, a slow, terrible unfolding of lips. She reached into her coat and withdrew a cigarette case—silver, engraved with the Morska crest. She lit it with a match struck against the basalt, the flare illuminating the staples in the Hulks' necks. "Bold," Mara murmured, exhaling a cloud of blue smoke that smelled of cloves and grave-dirt. "Stupid. But bold. Very well, *Lady* Aya. You negotiate." She snapped her fingers. "Bind the scholar and the girl. Throw them in the hold. If the Admiralty doesn't wire the transfer by the turn of the tide..." She drew a finger across her throat. "They feed the furnaces. And you?" She crouched, bringing the cigarette to Aya’s lips. Aya didn't flinch. She inhaled, the smoke bitter, grounding. "You," Mara whispered, blowing the smoke into Aya’s heterochromatic eyes, "come with me. We have a Key to turn. And I intend to see exactly what kind of monster you really are when the lights go out." The Hulks hauled Aya upright. The immateria roared in the sudden silence, a beast straining against a chain of her own making. She had bought them time. She had bought them life. But as the Warden led her toward the pulsing, screaming bone—toward the rift, toward the truth of what the Morska truly guarded—Aya knew with a cold certainty that the noose her mother wore was finally tightening around her own neck. And she had tied the knot herself.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing ability with vivid worldbuilding and atmospheric description. The author successfully creates a compelling "whalepunk" Victorian gothic setting with industrial elements like whale oil, brass fixtures, and steam-powered "Hulks" (reanimated corpses). The imagery is consistently evocative, from the opening description of air "clotting in the lungs like rendered blubber" to the artifact described as having a "slow, sick heartbeat of stolen starlight." The dialogue effectively captures distinct character voices. Mara's cold authority comes through in lines like "The game is over. The Key returns to the deep where it belongs," while Aya's aristocratic background shows in her formal speech patterns and strategic thinking. The conversation feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. The piece adheres well to the prompt's requirements, hitting all major story beats: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya is unmasked and captured, and she attempts to negotiate using her value as a hostage. The author successfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension and power dynamics. Character actions feel believable within the established world. Aya's quick thinking in leveraging her aristocratic status for survival fits her established intelligence and background. Mara's revelation as the true power behind events, having orchestrated her own "arrest," demonstrates cunning that aligns with her position. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought passages that border on purple prose. Descriptions occasionally become dense with metaphor and imagery that, while atmospheric, can slow pacing. The writing sometimes prioritizes style over clarity, particularly in action sequences where the Hulks capture the protagonists. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly in Aya's internal struggle between her aristocratic identity and her criminal activities, and her guilt over potentially exposing her companions to danger. The piece maintains consistent gothic horror tone throughout while building genuine tension about the characters' fates. The ending effectively sets up future conflict while resolving the immediate scene. Aya's realization that she may have "tied the knot herself" provides appropriate darkness without feeling forced. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 78.0
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon jukebox in the corner sputters "Sympathy for the Devil" for the fourth time tonight. The scratchy vinyl hiss competes with the hum of a dying refrigerator and the wet cough of the bartender polishing glasses with a rag that hasn't seen soap since the Carter administration. Spike Spiegel doesn't look up when the door bangs open. He knows the rhythm of this place—the irregular footsteps, the pause at the threshold, the scan. He's been sitting on this stool for three hours, nursing a whiskey that tastes like paint thinner and regret. The ice has long since surrendered. The newcomer's boots hit the floorboards with purpose. Heavy. Confident. Two pistols ride low on her hips, Cutlasses if he's not mistaken. Custom grips. She's small, compact, wearing shorts that violate several municipal codes and a crop top that reveals a dragon coiling up her right arm, scales catching the sickly neon light. Revy. Two Hands. The Lagoon Company's attack dog. She doesn't scan the room. She *reads* it. Eyes moving like a predator's—assessing, dismissing, filing away threats. They land on him. Pause. Narrow. "Well, *fuck*." Her voice cuts through the Stones cover like a straight razor. "Spike Spiegel. The ghost with the bad haircut." Spike finally turns. The prosthetic eye whirs almost imperceptibly as it adjusts focus. His left eye, the real one, holds that particular brand of exhausted amusement. "Revy. You're a long way from Roanapur." "Job brought me here. Same as you, I'm guessing." She slides onto the stool beside him, close enough that the scent of gun oil and cheap cigarettes and something floral beneath it all—jasmine, maybe—cuts through the bar's miasma. "Don't suppose you're here for the *White Orchid* bounty?" Spike's fingers tighten infinitesimally around his glass. "Maybe. Why? You looking to split the fee?" "I'm looking to *collect* the fee." She signals the bartender with two fingers. "Bourbon. Bottle. Leave it." When the man hesitates, she adds a glare that could strip paint. "Now." The bottle arrives. She pours a generous measure, knocks it back without ceremony, pours another. Spike watches the line of her throat work. "Target's a syndicate accountant named Chen," Spike says conversationally. "Skipped out with three million in encrypted drives. Last seen at the Kowloon Motel, room 304. Check-in was six hours ago." Revy's laugh is a bark. "You've got a source inside the Tongs?" "I've got a source inside a packet of instant ramen I ate for breakfast. Chen's wife called in the bounty herself. Wants him back before the syndicate decides he's a liability." He drains his glass. "She's paying double for discretion. Triple for alive." "Alive's boring." Revy swirls her bourbon, the amber liquid catching the jukebox's flickering red light. "Dead's cleaner. Less screaming." "Less money, too." "I don't do this for the money, Spike. You know that." He does. He knows the type. The ones who burn hot and bright and leave scorch marks on everyone close enough to feel the heat. He sees the old fractures in her—childhood carved into adult armor, trust a foreign currency she stopped accepting years ago. He carries his own fault lines. A woman named Julia. A syndicate called Red Dragon. A past he plays like a losing hand because folding means admitting the game matters. "Whatever happens, happens," he murmurs. Revy's head snaps toward him. Something flashes across her face—recognition, maybe. Or just the reflection of her own fatalism in someone else's eyes. "That your philosophy? Sounds like an excuse to stop giving a shit." "Sounds like acceptance. There's a difference." "Bullshit. Acceptance is what you tell yourself when you're too tired to fight anymore." She finishes her second pour. "I don't accept shit. I take what I want. I kill what's in my way. The rest is noise." "Even the noise that matters?" The question hangs between them, heavy as chambered rounds. The jukebox clicks, rewinds, starts the track over. *Please allow me to introduce myself...* Revy's mouth curves. Not a smile. Something sharper. "You're dangerous, Spiegel. Chatty. Philosophical. "Race you there." "Wouldn't be a race if I ran, would it?" He walks out into the night air, humid and thick with the promise of rain. Behind him, he hears the bar door slam. Footsteps—quick, light, gaining. He doesn't run. He doesn't need to. --- The Kowloon Motel reeks of mildew and desperation. Room 304's door hangs open, chain lock dangling uselessly. Inside: a man in his fifties, sweating through a cheap suit, frantically typing on a laptop connected to an external drive. Two bodies on the floor—syndicate cleanup crew, judging by the tattoos visible at their collars. Fresh kills. Still cooling. Chen doesn't look up. "You're late. The encryption—" "Save it." Revy's in the doorway, both Cutlasses drawn, stance wide and perfect. "Hands where I can see them. Drives on the bed. Now." Chen freezes. His eyes dart past her—to Spike, leaning against the frame with a cigarette dangling from his lips, unlit. Hands in his pockets. Utterly relaxed. "Two hunters," Chen whispers. "They sent *two*." "One's plenty," Spike says around the cigarette. "The other's just... competitive." Revy doesn't glance back. "Stay out of this, Spike. This one's mine. Alive, dead—I don't give a rat's ass. But the payday's mine." "Triple for alive, remember? Wife's orders." He finally lights the cigarette, the flare brief and orange in the dim room. "You kill him, you get the base rate. Barely covers your bar tab." "I'll make it up on the next job. And the one after that." Her finger tightens on the left trigger. "Last chance, accountant. Drives. Bed. *Now*." Chen's hand hovers over the keyboard. His eyes flick between them—calculating, desperate. A cornered rat with data worth millions. "Or," Spike says, "you hand over the drives, we split the triple fee three ways, and you disappear. New face, new name, new life. My guy can have papers ready in twelve hours." Revy's head whips around. "You're *negotiating*? With a *mark*?" "I'm solving a problem. You're creating one." Spike pushes off the doorframe, taking a slow step forward. "Chen. Drives. Bed. You walk out the back. My contact meets you at the docks. Midnight. *Seahorse* freighter, container seven." "And if I don't trust you?" Chen's voice cracks. "Then you trust her." Spike nods at Revy. "She kills you. Syndicate gets the drives anyway. Your wife gets nothing. Your daughter's medical bills go unpaid." He exhales smoke. "Your call." The silence stretches. The jukebox downstairs is audible through the floorboards—*Sympathy for the Devil* again, the same scratchy loop. Somewhere, a baby cries. A couple argues in rapid Cantonese. Chen's shoulders slump. He ejects the drive, places it on the bed. Stands slowly, hands raised. "The... the encryption key. It's in my pocket. Left side." Spike moves like water—close, retrieve, verify. A small USB drive. He tosses it to Revy. She catches it one-handed, doesn't lower her guns. "Back door's clear," Spike tells Chen. "Go. Don't look back." Chen doesn't need telling twice. He scrambles past them, out the rear exit, the screen door slapping shut behind him. Silence in the room. Two hunters. One bounty. Three million credits. Revy holsters her right pistol. Left stays trained on Spike's center mass. "You just gave away a third of our cut." "Our cut? *Your* cut. I don't need the money." "Bullshit. You're always broke. Jet complains about it constantly. That ship of yours is held together by duct tape and prayers." "Bebop's a classic. Character." He takes a drag, blows smoke toward the ceiling fan. "Besides. Money's just numbers. Freedom's what matters." "Freedom." The word comes out like a curse. "You keep using that word. I don't think it means what you think it means." "What does it mean to you, then?" Revy's jaw works. The dragon on her arm seems to shift as her muscles tense. "Freedom's not owing anyone a goddamn thing. Not a syndicate. Not a crew. Not some past you can't outrun no matter how fast you fly." Her voice drops, raw. "It's waking up and knowing the only person who decides if you live or die is *you*." Spike's real eye meets hers. The prosthetic whirs. "And if someone else decides for you?" "Then you make them *regret it*." She steps closer. The gun doesn't waver. "You make them pay in blood and fear and you keep walking." "Even if it destroys you?" "Especially then." The space between them has vanished. Close enough to feel heat radiating off her skin. Close enough to see the fine tremors in her shooting hand—not fear, never fear. Adrenaline. Anticipation. Something that looks a lot like want wearing violence's clothes. Spike's cigarette burns down to the filter. He drops it, grinds it out with his heel. "You're trouble, Revy." "Takes one to know one, *cowboy*." The honorific drips with mockery. With challenge. With something neither will name. His hand moves—not to his gun, but to the back of her neck, fingers tangling in dark hair. She doesn't pull away. Doesn't shoot. Her free hand fists in his shirt, yanking him down, and their mouths collide like a car wreck—teeth and tongue and desperation, tasting of bourbon and cigarettes and something that might be hope if hope weren't a four-letter word for suicide. The gun pressed against his ribs doesn't fire. His hand on her throat doesn't squeeze. The jukebox downstairs clicks, rewinds, starts again. *Please allow me to introduce myself...* They break apart breathing hard, foreheads touching. Gun still at his ribs. Hand still at her throat. "Motel room's paid through morning," Spike murmurs. "Thin walls. Cheap sheets. No questions asked." Revy's laugh is low, rough. "Thought you didn't do attachments." "I don't. This isn't attachment. This is..." He searches for the word, comes up empty. "This is whatever happens." "Whatever happens, happens." She echoes him, bitter and hungry. "Fine. But if you try to play the hero—if you try to *save* me—I'll put a bullet in your prosthetic eye and watch you bleed out on these nasty sheets." "Wouldn't dream of it." "Good." She shoves him back, holsters both guns in one fluid motion. "Race you to the bed. Loser buys breakfast." "You're on." The neon sign outside flickers—KOWLOON MOTEL, the O burning out, the N sputtering. Inside, two damaged people who've spent lifetimes running from themselves collide in the dark, and for a few hours, the running stops. The jukebox plays on.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing ability and solid character work within the noir/action genre. The author successfully captures the distinctive voices and mannerisms of both Spike and Revy, maintaining their canonical personalities while creating believable chemistry between them. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Spike's laconic philosophy contrasting effectively against Revy's aggressive pragmatism. The atmospheric writing is particularly strong, establishing the seedy bar and motel settings with vivid sensory details that enhance the noir mood. The author shows good restraint in building tension, allowing the sexual and violent undercurrents to simmer without becoming overwrought. The pacing moves smoothly from the initial meeting through the job completion to the final standoff. However, the piece suffers from some structural issues. The bounty hunt resolution feels somewhat rushed and convenient - Chen's quick capitulation and Spike's sudden offer of escape papers comes across as expedient plotting rather than organic development. The philosophical exchanges, while true to Spike's character, occasionally veer toward pretentious territory without fully earning their weight. The ending, while appropriately unresolved given the characters' natures, feels slightly anticlimactic. The transition from gunpoint standoff to sexual tension resolves too easily, lacking the complexity such damaged characters would realistically bring to intimacy. The repeated jukebox motif, while atmospheric, becomes somewhat heavy-handed by the conclusion. The prose quality is generally high, with strong imagery and natural sentence flow, though it occasionally indulges in noir clichés. The character work is the piece's strongest element - both protagonists feel authentic and their mutual attraction develops believably through their shared cynicism and professional respect. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 76.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The church bell had no business ringing at midnight. No service, no holiday, no funeral announced in the weekly bulletin Mama pinned to the kitchen corkboard beside the ICA receipts and Papa's overtime schedules. Just the one clear tone rolling across the valley, over the tar-paper roofs of Granviken, through the spruce stands and the peat bogs, finding us where we crouched on the burial mound. I heard it in my sternum before my ears caught up. "Did you hear that?" I whispered. Astrid didn't look up from the matchbox. Her fingers, pale against the striking strip, held the match at the exact angle her mormor had shown her. Forty-five degrees. Strike away from the body. Let the sulfur burn off before you touch it to the wick. "Klockan," she said. "It does that sometimes." "The bell doesn't ring at midnight." "Then it's not midnight." Her voice was flat, bored, the same tone she used to correct my Swedish when I said *köra* instead of *åka* for taking the bus. As if the bell, the mound, the whole northern dark were simply facts she'd memorized for a test she'd already passed. The match flared. Sulfur smell, sharp and old. She touched it to the candle stub wedged into a crack in the mound's flank—beeswax, she'd said, not paraffin. *Paraffin comes from oil. Oil comes from dead things pressed down. Beeswax comes from living things building up.* Her mormor's words, delivered while they melted down tapers in a tin can over a spirit stove in Astrid's kitchen, the air thick with honey-smoke and something else I couldn't name. Pine resin, maybe. Or the dried herbs tied in bundles from the rafters: yarrow, mugwort, angelica root. *Ängsikt, alvklingan, kvann.* Meadowsweet, elf-bell, angelica. Protection plants. Or invitation plants. Astrid had used both words interchangeably. "Sit," she said. "Don't cross your ankles. Don't interlock your fingers. Palms on your knees, facing up. Spine straight but not rigid. Like you're a vessel." "A vessel for what?" "Whatever comes." I did as instructed. The mound was cold through my jeans, the wool sweater Mama had knitted, the thermal underwear she'd insisted on despite my protests that I wasn't *barn* anymore. Fifteen years old and dressed for an arctic expedition in late September. The grass smelled of frost and old iron. Beneath that, something sweet and rotting. *Jordgubbar*, Astrid had called it when I wrinkled my nose. *Strawberries. The earth smells like strawberries when the dead wake up.* "Now what?" "Now we wait. We don't speak. We don't look at each other. We look at the horizon—there, where the treeline meets the sky. You'll see it change." "See what change?" "The boundary. *Gränsen.* It thins at midnight. On the mounds especially. The old ones knew. They built them high for a reason. Closer to the stars. Closer to the *väsen*." "Väsen. Beings. Spirits." "Don't translate. Translation loses the weight. *Väsen* comes from *vara*—to be. The ones who *are*. Not ghosts. Not dead. They never lived like us. They're the ones who were here before the first person put a plow in the ground." The candle flame guttered. No wind I could feel. The treeline was a black serration against a sky so dense with stars it looked bruised, purple-black and swollen. No moon. *Mörkmåne*, Astrid had said. Dark moon. The best time. Or the worst. She'd smiled when she said it, the flash of teeth in her kitchen's fluorescent light. My knees ached. The cold crept up my spine, vertebra by vertebra. Somewhere in the valley a dog barked once, short and sharp, then cut off. An owl—*ugla*, not *uggla*, Astrid had corrected me—called from the spruces. *Hu-hu-hu-hu.* Low. Mournful. Human, almost. *Don't look at each other. Don't speak.* My mind filled with the silence. School on Monday. Erik Lindqvist's locker two down from mine, the way he smelled of lynx deodorant and woodsmoke. The note I'd written and torn up. The way Mama had cried silently at the kitchen table three weeks ago, Papa's transfer letter in her hands, the life in Stockholm dissolving like sugar in hot coffee. *Det blir bra, Linnea. Det blir en ny början.* It'll be good. A new beginning. *Gränsen.* The stars seemed to vibrate. Not move—vibrate. A hum at the edge of hearing, felt in the teeth and the fingertips. The candle flame stretched tall and blue, burning without flicker. *Astrid.* I didn't turn my head. Peripheral vision only: her profile sharp against the star-field, eyes fixed on the horizon, mouth slightly parted. Not breathing. Or breathing so shallow the cold air didn't condense. Something moved in the treeline. Not an animal. Not wind in branches. A shape—tall, elongated, moving *against* the slope of the ground. Uphill without effort. No footsteps. No sound but the owl, still calling, *hu-hu-hu-hu*, and now a second answering from deeper in the forest. *Don't look at each other.* I looked. The shape resolved into a man. Or the idea of a man. Tall as a pine, shoulders broad as a doorframe, but the proportions wrong—limbs too long, joints bending the wrong way. He wore something dark, wool maybe, a cap pulled low. He carried nothing. He approached the mound directly, not picking a path, not hesitating at the tussocks or the hidden stones. My throat closed. My palms, facing up on my knees, prickled with pins and needles. *Don't speak.* "Är du redo?" The voice came from beside me—Astrid, whispering, breaking her own rule. *Are you ready?* The figure stopped at the mound's base. Ten meters. Five. The candle flame went out. Not blown. Not snuffed. *Gone.* Darkness absolute. The stars vanished. The treeline vanished. Only the mound beneath me, the cold seeping through denim and wool and skin, and the presence looming above—close enough that I felt the displacement of air, the pressure change in my ears. A hand touched my forehead. Dry. Cold as river water in April. Fingers—too many, too long—traced a line from brow to chin, down the throat, over the sternum. Stopped at my heart. *Väsen.* The owl screamed. A sound like a woman being murdered, my grandmother in Stockholm would have said. *Skogsrået.* The forest woman. But this wasn't a woman. This was old. Older than the forest. Older than the mound. "Linnea." My name. Spoken without voice. Spoken inside the bone. The hand withdrew. The pressure lifted. The stars slammed back into existence, violent and bright. The candle reignited itself—blue flame, tall and steady. The figure was gone. No retreat. No footsteps fading. Simply *not there* where it had been *there*. Astrid exhaled beside me, a long shuddering breath. Her shoulders dropped. She looked at me, really looked, for the first time that night. Her face was pale, sweat beading at her hairline despite the cold. "Did you—" "Don't," I said. My voice didn't sound like mine. "Don't ask." She nodded. Once. Serious now, the boredom burned away. "We have to close it properly. Walk backwards down the mound. Nine steps. Don't turn around until your feet touch the flat ground. Then we run. Don't look back. Don't speak until we're inside with the door locked." "Nine steps?" "Nine is the number of *hel*. The underworld. We're returning from a visit." I stood. Legs shaking. Pins and needles screaming up from my feet. *One.* The grass crunched under my boot. *Two.* The owl fell silent. *Three.* A whisper in my ear—*not Astrid's voice, not any voice*—*kom igen.* Come again. *Four. Five. Six.* The church bell rang again. One tone. Midnight. Or one past. Or the bell simply ringing because something had passed through the boundary and the old iron knew. *Seven. Eight. Nine.* Flat ground. I turned. Astrid was already running, a dark shape tearing toward the village lights. I followed, lungs burning, the mound shrinking behind us, the candle still burning blue on its flank—a beacon, or a warning, or an invitation left carelessly open. We didn't speak until we were in her bedroom, the door locked, the heavy curtains drawn against the star-swollen sky. Her hands shook as she poured water from a chipped enamel pitcher. Mine shook taking the mug. "Mormor said the first time is always the hardest," Astrid said. She sat on the edge of her bed, mug cradled between both hands. "She said the *väsen* test you. See if you're *värdig*. Worthy. Or just... curious." "Was I worthy?" She looked at me over the rim. The kitchen light caught her eyes—brown, flecked with gold, old eyes in a fifteen-year-old face. "You're still here. You didn't scream. You didn't run before the nine steps." She set down the mug. "But *Linnea*... worthy isn't the same as safe. Nothing about this is safe." Outside, the wind rose. The spruces groaned. Somewhere in the valley, a dog began to howl, long and low, joined by another, and another, a chorus rising toward the dark moon. I pressed my palm to my chest, over the place where the cold fingers had rested. The skin was warm. Normal. But underneath, in the bone, a fingerprint of frost remained—would remain, I knew with sudden terrible certainty, for the rest of my life. "Teach me," I said. "The closing ritual. The protection plants. Everything." Astrid smiled. It wasn't a nice smile. It was the smile of someone who has just won a game she didn't know she was playing. "Tomorrow night," she said. "We do *galdr*. Sound magic. You'll need to learn the runes." The church bell didn't ring again. But I heard it in my dreams for years after—one clear tone at midnight, calling me back to the mound, to the boundary, to the things that *are* waiting for someone to sit still long enough to listen.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing that effectively captures the folk horror genre. The author successfully establishes the rural Swedish setting through authentic details like ICA receipts, Swedish vocabulary, and cultural references. The first-person retrospective narration works well, creating appropriate distance while maintaining immediacy. The characterization is nuanced, particularly Linnea's portrayal as a displaced Stockholm teenager caught between skepticism and fascination. Her internal conflict feels genuine - the homesickness, cultural adjustment, and teenage desire to belong all ring true. Astrid is effectively portrayed as knowledgeable yet potentially manipulative, with her matter-of-fact delivery of occult information creating an unsettling contrast. The prose quality is generally high, with evocative sensory details and strong atmospheric building. The author effectively uses Swedish terms and folklore elements, creating authenticity without over-explaining. The pacing builds tension well, moving from preparation through the ritual to the climactic encounter. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought passages, particularly in the supernatural encounter sequence. Phrases like "stars slammed back into existence, violent and bright" and "star-swollen sky" veer toward purple prose. The supernatural elements, while maintaining appropriate ambiguity, occasionally feel heavy-handed rather than subtly unsettling. The dialogue serves its purpose but lacks distinctive character voices - both girls speak in similar patterns. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat predictable in its "corruption of innocence" trajectory. The piece succeeds in maintaining the crucial ambiguity between psychological and supernatural explanations, though it leans more heavily supernatural than might be ideal for folk horror. The cultural details and ritual elements feel researched and authentic, contributing to the overall effectiveness.
