+ Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The boulder didn’t care about the column. The boulder didn’t care about the growing stack of scrolls tied to the olive tree, or the inkpot wedged into a cleft of rock, or the fact that Sisyphus had developed a callus on his right forefinger from gripping a reed pen instead of a lump of granite. The boulder just wanted to go down. Sisyphus let it go. He stepped aside with the easy grace of a man who has sidestepped several thousand tonnes of sedimentary rock over three millennia, dusting his hands on his chiton. "Right then," he said to the empty air. "Where were we?" "‘Desperate in Delphi’," croaked a voice from the olive tree. "The one about the mother-in-law and the olive oil." A large, glossy crow hopped down from a branch, clutching a scroll in one claw. He looked like a feathered inkwell that had seen too much. This was Crow. He didn’t speak so much as project syllables into the atmosphere with a distinct lack of enthusiasm. "Ah, yes. The oil." Sisyphus took the scroll, squinting at the cramped handwriting. "‘Dear Sisyphus, my husband’s mother visits quarterly and insists on reorganizing my kitchen. Last week she replaced my cooking oil with her own ‘blessed’ blend. My spanakopita tasted like incense. I want to scream. Am I petty?’" He scratched his beard, the gesture slow, deliberate. "Crow. Dictation." Crow sighed, a sound like dry leaves skittering on stone. He pulled a fresh sheet of papyrus from the satchel slung over his shoulder and poised a charcoal stick. "‘Dear Desperate,’" Sisyphus began, his voice warm, rumbling slightly in his chest. "‘You are not petty. You are territorial. There is a difference. Petty is stealing her sandals. Territorial is drawing a line in the flour on the counter. Tell her, gently but firmly, that your kitchen is your temple. If she wishes to bless the oil, she may bless it in her own amphora, in her own house. Offer her a jar of the good stuff to take home. It costs three drachmas. Your peace of mind costs more. Keep the receipt. Yours, Sisyphus.’" Crow scratched away, feathers ruffling. "You’re soft on the in-laws." "I’m practical on the in-laws," Sisyphus corrected, walking back to the base of the slope where the boulder waited, patient as a sleeping dog. "Fighting them is pushing uphill. Redirecting them is leverage. Next." "‘Confused in Corinth’," Crow read, hopping alongside him. "‘I work fourteen hours a day at the pottery. My wife says I don’t listen. I *do* listen. I hear the clay, the wheel, the kiln. She says that’s not what she means. What does she mean?’" Sisyphus placed his hands on the cold, rough curve of the stone. He didn't heave. Not yet. He just leaned, feeling the weight settle into his shoulders, his legs, the arches of his feet. "‘Dear Confused,’" he dictated, not turning his head. "‘She doesn’t mean the noise. She means the silence. The silence between you when you come home and the clay is still under your fingernails. She’s not asking you to work less. She’s asking you to arrive when you get home. Wash your hands. Look at her face. Ask her about *her* kiln. The pots will still be there tomorrow. She might not be. Yours, Sisyphus.’" Crow tapped the charcoal against the papyrus. "Bit domestic for a King of Corinth, isn't it?" "Kings give orders," Sisyphus said, the first strain tightening his jaw as the boulder broke its static friction and began to roll. "Advice columnists give perspectives. Different muscles. *Heave.*" The boulder groaned upward. Sisyphus moved with it, a dance of inertia and intent. "‘Lonely in Lesbos’," Crow called out, flapping heavily to keep pace, the satchel bouncing. "‘I’ve tried every dating app. Well, the one app. The messenger pigeon service. Three dates. One stole my signet ring. One talked only about his trireme. One wept into his kykeon about his ex. I’m considering a vow of chastity and a goat herd. Advice?’" Sisyphus breathed in rhythm with the slope. *Push. Step. Push. Step.* The gradient steepened. "‘Dear Lonely,’" he said, voice steady despite the exertion. "‘Don’t buy the goats yet. Goats are louder than bad dates and harder to shoo out of the bedroom. The ring thief wanted your status. The trireme bore wanted an audience. The weeper wanted a therapist. None of them wanted *you*. That’s not a failure of the market. That’s data. You’ve learned three things you don’t want. Cross them off. Go to the market on Tuesday. Buy the figs you like. Talk to the woman who sells the honey. She laughs at her own jokes. That’s a start. Yours, Sisyphus.’" "‘P.S. The goats are a backup plan, not a retirement strategy,’" Crow added on his own. "Strike the P.S., Crow." "Already inked." Sisyphus grunted as the path narrowed, the rock face closing in. "‘Anxious in Athens’," Crow read the next scroll, unrolling it with a claw. "‘I feel like I’m just… turning a handle. Grinding grain for people who eat the bread and complain about the crust. What is the *point*? I don’t mean philosophically. I mean Tuesday morning.’" The boulder hit a patch of loose shale. Sisyphus adjusted his stance instantly, toes gripping, weight shifting low. He didn't slip. "‘Dear Anxious,’" Sisyphus said, sweat beading on his forehead now, dripping into his eyes. He didn't wipe it. "‘The point isn’t the bread. The point isn’t even the grain. The point is the rhythm. You find the rhythm in the handle, and you own the rhythm. The complainers don’t own the rhythm. They just eat the toast. You’re the one turning. That’s not nothing. That’s the only thing that’s *yours*. Yours, Sisyphus.’" Crow was silent for a long moment, wings beating slow. "That one was close to the bone, Boss." "Which bone?" "The one about the rhythm." Sisyphus smiled, a crinkling at the corners of his eyes. "It’s not a metaphor, Crow. It’s just physics. If you fight the weight, you break. If you *are* the weight moving… you’re just moving." "Right. Physics." Crow pecked at the next scroll. "‘Frisky in Phocis.’ Oh, for—" "Read it." "‘Dear Sisyphus. My husband and I have been married twenty years. The spark is gone. We’ve tried oils, positions, the Kama Sutra scroll (the illustrated one, very sticky), roleplay—I was a priestess, he was a Minotaur, it ended with a horn in the eye. We just… fold laundry. How do we get the folding *exciting* again?’" Sisyphus crested the ridge. The plateau stretched flat and golden before them, the olive tree a dark smudge against the sunset. The boulder slowed, the gradient easing. He gave it one final, easy shove to park it in its designated hollow. It settled with a sigh of dust. He wiped his forehead now. "‘Dear Frisky,’" he dictated, leaning against the warm flank of the stone, catching his breath. "‘You’re asking the wrong question. You don’t want exciting folding. Exciting folding leads to torn tunics and lost socks. You want *intentional* folding. Tonight, don’t fold the laundry. Leave it in the basket. Pour two cups of that rough red wine you hide behind the amphora. Sit on the floor. Touch his hand. Don’t talk about the Minotaur. Talk about the first time you saw him fold a shirt. Stay there until the wine is gone. The laundry will wait. It always does. Yours, Sisyphus.’" "Sentimental old fool," Crow muttered, rolling up the scroll and tying it to a leg. "You used to cheat Death. Now you give relationship advice involving cheap wine." "Cheating Death was cardio," Sisyphus said, stretching his back. "This is maintenance. More useful." A shimmer of displaced air. The smell of ozone and expensive sandalwood. Sisyphus didn't turn. He knew that scent. It smelled like a budget meeting on Olympus. "Sisyphus." "Hermes. Or a very lost perfume salesman." Sisyphus picked up a waterskin. The messenger god materialized on the path, winged sandals gleaming, caduceus clicking against his thigh. He looked harassed. He always looked harassed. "Zeus has seen the scrolls." "Did he like the one about the spanakopita?" "He calls it ‘unauthorized dissemination of divine justice narratives.’ He says you’re ‘trivializing the deterrent.’" Hermes tapped a scroll case against his palm. "Also, Hera wants to know who ‘Desperate in Delphi’ is. She’s taking notes." "Tell Zeus the deterrent works fine. The boulder’s still here. I’m still here." Sisyphus took a long drink. "Tell Hera Desperate is a metaphor. We’re all Desperate in Delphi, Hermes. Some of us just have better olive oil." Hermes snorted, a short, sharp sound. "He wants you to cease and desist. Or at least add a disclaimer. ‘The views expressed do not reflect the management of Tartarus Inc.’" "Crow," Sisyphus said. "Take a letter to Zeus." Crow groaned, preening a primary feather. "He doesn't read mail. He throws thunderbolts at it." "Then I’ll keep it brief." Sisyphus picked up a shard of pottery and scratched on a fresh scrap of papyrus. "‘Dear Management. Re: Trivialization. The deterrent remains fully operational. The boulder goes up. The boulder goes down. The column goes out. The people feel heard. Everyone does their job. Stop micromanaging the help. Regards, The Rock.’" He held it out. Hermes stared at it. Then at Sisyphus. Then at the boulder, sitting innocuous in its hollow. "You're insubordinate," Hermes said, but there was a grudging grin tugging at his mouth. "You're *enjoying* this." "I'm *useful*," Sisyphus corrected gently. "There's a difference. Tell Zeus he should try it sometime. Answer a prayer. Just one. See how it sits." Hermes took the scrap, tucking it into his belt. "He'll blast it. But… I'll deliver it. Personally." He glanced at the stack of outgoing scrolls tied to the olive tree. "‘Frisky in Phocis.’ Good advice. The wine trick. Does that work?" "Works on everyone but gods," Sisyphus said. "You lot have ichor instead of blood. No tolerance." Hermes laughed, a bright, sharp sound that scattered the twilight shadows. "Right. Well. Keep the deterrent deterring. And… tell the bird to write legibly. The Fates complain about his handwriting when they do the cross-referencing." "Will do." Sisyphus watched him blur away, a streak of gold and blue. Crow landed on the boulder, shaking out his wings. "He’s gone. You’re still here. The boulder’s still here. The inbox is full." "Always is," Sisyphus said. He picked up the next scroll from the 'Urgent' pile. "‘Worried in Thebes. My teenage son speaks only in grunts and thinks the gorgon next door is ‘hot.’’" "Teenagers," Crow said sympathetically. "Worse than hydras. At least hydras have the decency to grow back when you chop them." "‘Dear Worried,’" Sisyphus dictated, settling back against the warm stone as the first stars pricked the velvet dark. "‘The gorgon is a phase. The grunts are a language. Learn the grammar. Bring snacks. Don’t make eye contact with the snakes. Yours, Sisyphus.’" He paused. The night air was cool on his sweat-damp skin. The boulder radiated the day's heat, a slow, steady release. "Crow?" "Yeah, Boss?" "Leave the boulder metaphor in the 'Anxious in Athens' one. The rhythm bit." Crow blinked a beady eye. "Thought we agreed. No boulder metaphors. Cliché. Hackneyed. 'Pratchett would hate it.' Your words." Sisyphus smiled into the dark. "It’s not a metaphor, Crow. It’s just the address. Let them know where the letter came from." "Right. The address." Crow scratched the final line. *‘P.S. The view from the top is just a view. The view from the push is the whole world.’* "Good bird," Sisyphus said. "Now, about that goat herd…"
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of both the prompt requirements and Terry Pratchett's distinctive style. The author successfully creates an epistolary advice column format while maintaining narrative momentum through the physical action of boulder-pushing and character interactions. The characterization of Sisyphus is particularly well-executed. Rather than the expected bitter or overly philosophical figure, he emerges as genuinely warm, practical, and surprisingly adept at human psychology. His advice feels earned through experience rather than academic knowledge, and his responses show real emotional intelligence. The relationship with Crow provides excellent comedic relief while serving the practical function of scribe, and their banter feels natural and lived-in. The Pratchettesque humor is well-calibrated - understated rather than forced, emerging from character interactions and situational absurdity rather than obvious jokes. Lines like "Goats are louder than bad dates and harder to shoo out of the bedroom" capture Pratchett's blend of the mundane and absurd perfectly. The author wisely avoids over-reliance on boulder metaphors while allowing one subtle instance to slip through naturally. The advice letters themselves are cleverly varied, ranging from domestic disputes to existential concerns to relationship issues, each receiving thoughtful, practical responses that feel genuinely helpful rather than preachy. The progression from simple domestic issues to more complex emotional territory shows good pacing. The prose style successfully mimics Pratchett's voice - conversational yet precise, with excellent use of physical detail and character gesture to convey personality. The integration of the boulder-pushing with the advice-giving creates a natural rhythm that mirrors Sisyphus's own acceptance of his routine. The appearance of Hermes provides effective external conflict and world-building, showing how this new venture fits into the larger mythological framework. The exchange feels authentic to both characters and adds stakes without overwhelming the gentle tone. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Occasionally the dialogue becomes slightly exposition-heavy, particularly in Hermes's scene where he delivers Zeus's concerns. Some of the advice, while well-intentioned, borders on being too neat or pat in its solutions. The ending, while charming, feels slightly rushed compared to the careful pacing of the earlier sections. The piece succeeds admirably in its primary goals: creating believable character growth, maintaining Pratchett's tone, and delivering genuinely engaging content that subverts expectations while remaining true to the mythological source material. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in Den Den Town smelled of ozone, frying oil, and the distinct, dusty perfume of vintage capacitors. Riko loved it. It was the only place where the noise inside her head matched the noise outside. She stood on tiptoe in the cramped aisle of *Super Potato*, her fingers hovering over a yellowed Roland SH-101. The price tag made her stomach twist—eighty thousand yen. Eighty thousand yen for a plastic box that went *bweep* and *bwoop*. She’d calculated it: three months of convenience store night shifts. Four, if she actually ate. "Testing, testing. One, two, three... *shred*." The sound cut through the shop’s ambient hum. Not a synth. A guitar. Electric. High gain, sharp attack, but clean articulation. Riko didn’t move her hand from the SH-101, but her head turned, radar pinging. It was the *Evangelion* theme. *A Cruel Angel’s Thesis*. But not the karaoke version. This was the instrumental arrangement from the *Renewal* soundtrack—Yoko Takahashi’s vocal melody transcribed for lead guitar, harmonized thirds screaming over a double-kick drum backing track blasting from a small battery-powered amp. Riko left the synth. She didn't remember deciding to walk. She just drifted, carried by the current of the melody, past the retro game cabinets, past the maid cafe flyers, out onto the narrow street where the afternoon sun caught the steam rising from a takoyaki grill. The busker sat on a folding stool near the entrance of the Taito Station arcade. She looked older. Twenty, maybe twenty-one. Doc Martens scuffed at the toes. Oversized vintage Slayer tee tucked into high-waisted shorts. A cascade of bleached hair with dark roots showing, held back by a bandana. A Fender Jaguar hung low on her hip, sunburst finish catching the light. She wasn't just playing the notes. She was *inside* them. Her eyes were closed, mouth slightly open, body swaying. When the solo hit—the frantic, neoclassical run—her fingers didn't look like they were moving. The guitar just *screamed*. Riko stopped three meters back. She clutched her canvas tote bag (patches: *Korg, Moog, Serial Experiments Lain*) against her chest. A shield. The final chord rang out, feedback swelling, controlled, dying into silence. The busker opened her eyes. Dark eyeliner, sharp wings. She scanned the small crowd—salarymen checking watches, tourists filming, a kid eating a melon pan. Her gaze snagged on Riko. "Yo," the busker said. She didn't shout. She just spoke, and the mic on the amp stand picked it up. "Thanks for listening. Tip jar’s open. Venmo, PayPay, cold hard cash, high-fives accepted." People scattered. The spell broken by the transaction. Riko stayed. Her throat clicked. "You... you played the harmonized thirds in the B-section," Riko said. Her voice was thin, swallowed by the traffic on Sakaisuji. "Most people just play the root notes. Power chords. It’s easier." The busker grinned. It was a wide, sharp expression. She unplugged the cable from the Jaguar with a *thunk*, silencing the amp. "Most people don't have ears like yours. Or they're too busy filming for TikTok to hear the counter-melody." She stood up, stretching, the guitar hanging by its strap. Up close, she was taller than Riko. Intimidatingly cool. Riko took a half-step back, bumping into a lamppost. "I'm Hana," the busker said. She offered a hand—calloused fingertips, chipped black nail polish. "Full-time noise maker. Part-time convenience store ghost. You?" "Riko." Riko took the hand. Her own palm was sweaty. She wiped it on her jeans *after* letting go. "I... I don't have money. For the tip jar. I spent it. Almost. On an SH-101. Inside." Hana laughed. A bark of surprise. "An SH-101? In *this* economy? Bold. Respect. You a keyboardist?" "Synths," Riko corrected automatically, then winced. "I mean... synthesizers. Programming. Sequencing. Not... performing. I don't perform." "Smart," Hana said. She folded the stool with a practiced *clack*, slinging it over her shoulder. "Performing is just anxiety with an audience. Why do it for free when you can suffer alone in your bedroom?" Riko blinked. "That’s... exactly it. Bedroom. Suffering. Yes." "Kindred spirit," Hana declared. She started walking, gesturing for Riko to follow. "Come on, Riko-with-the-good-ears. I’m starving. You eat?" "Y-yes." "Good. There’s a *kaitenzushi* place two blocks over. *Sushiro*. The plates are a hundred yen. The tea is free. The wasabi is nuclear. My treat. Consider it payment for the music criticism." "I can't let you—" "Consider it an investment in the local music scene," Hana interrupted smoothly, navigating the crowd like a shark through minnows. Riko scrambled to keep up, tote bag bouncing. "I need a bassist for a session next week. You look like you know where the 'root note' lives." "I don't play bass," Riko said, breathless. "I program MIDI. Velocity curves. CC data. Envelope generators." "Even better. You speak robot. I speak noise. We need a translator." Hana glanced back, walking backwards now, dangerously close to a bicycle. "So. *Evangelion*. That your jam? Or just the one you recognized?" Riko hesitated. The question was a trap. Or a test. "It’s... the *Renewal* arrangement. 2003. Toshiyuki Ohmori arranged the strings. The guitar part you played... it’s an adaptation of the violin line. Measure forty-two. The pickup into the chorus. You slid the ninth fret to the twelfth on the B string. Vibrato width: approximately one semitone. Rate: fast." Hana stopped dead on the sidewalk. A salaryman shoulder-checked her. She didn't move. She turned, eyes wide, the playful mask slipping into something genuine. Hungry. "Measure forty-two," she repeated slowly. "Pickup. Ninth to twelfth. B string. Vibrato width. Rate." Riko shrank. "I... I have the sheet music. PDF. I analyzed the spectral centroid for a filter sweep I was designing. For a patch. On the SH-101. Hypothetically." "You're a weirdo," Hana said. The grin returned, softer now. Realer. "I like you. Come on. Sushi. Now. Tell me about the filter sweep." They slid into a booth at *Sushiro* ten minutes later. The conveyor belt hummed, a lazy river of shrimp, tuna, egg, and kappa maki. Hana immediately grabbed a green tea powder dispenser, tapping it furiously into a tiny ceramic cup, then pouring hot water from the spout at the table. "Matcha technique," she explained, whisking it with a disposable chopstick. "Froth is life. So. Filter sweep. Talk." Riko sat on her hands. The booth vinyl was cold. "It’s... a low-pass filter. 24dB per octave. Resonance high. Self-oscillating. I use the envelope generator to open the cutoff frequency *after* the note triggers. Slow attack. So the note starts muffled. Dark. Then... it blooms. Brightens. Like a flower. Or a scream waking up." She stopped, face burning. "It’s stupid. It’s just a preset idea." Hana set down the chopstick. She picked up a plate of *otoro*—fatty tuna—dipped it in the soy sauce dish (way too much wasabi, Riko noted), and ate it in one bite. She chewed thoughtfully. "Not stupid," Hana said. "That’s *timbre*. That’s emotion. Most guitarists just buy a distortion pedal and call it 'feeling.' You're sculpting the air. That's composition." She grabbed a plate of salmon roe. *Ikura*. "You know the *Haibane Renmei* soundtrack? Kou Otani?" Riko’s head snapped up. Her hands unclenched. "Yes. The guitar. The... the nylon string. *Refrain of Memory*. The way the reverb tail doesn't decay linearly. It gates. It breathes." "Exactly." Hana pointed a chopstick at her, *ikura* glistening. "Track three. *Free Bird*. Not the Lynyrd Skynyrd one. The ambient piece. The synth pad underneath the guitar... it does what you said. It *blooms*. Slow attack. High resonance. It sounds like wings unfolding." Riko stared. "I... I have a patch based on that. I call it 'Grey Feathers.' I’ve never... nobody knows that soundtrack. It’s obscure. Old. 2002." "Obscure is where the good stuff lives," Hana said. She leaned back, crossing her arms, looking satisfied. "Mainstream is just consensus. Consensus is boring. You, Riko... you listen to the decay. You listen to the space between the notes." She flagged down a passing plate of *tamago* (sweet egg), snagging it. "Okay. New plan. You finish your tea. We go back to Den Den Town. I buy you that SH-101—kidding, I'm broke. But I *will* help you haggle the guy down. Then you come to my practice space. Basement in Nipponbashi. Damp. Smells like mold and dreams. You bring 'Grey Feathers.' I bring the Jaguar. We see what happens when 'bloom' meets 'scream.'" Riko looked at the conveyor belt. A plate of *uni* (sea urchin) trundled past, expensive and orange. She looked at Hana—sharp eyeliner, Slayer shirt, *Haibane Renmei* in her pocket, offering a basement and a collaboration like it was a convenience store onigiri. The anxiety was still there. A low hum in her chest. 60-cycle hum. Ground loop. But underneath it... a new oscillator. A sine wave. Pure. Steady. "Okay," Riko said. She picked up her tea cup, blew on the foam. "But... I don't play well. With others. I quantize everything. I fix the timing. I make it perfect." Hana stood up, tossing her empty plates into the return slot. "Perfection is a grid, Riko. Life is swing. Come on. Let's make some glorious mistakes." She held out a hand. Not for a handshake. For a pull up. Riko looked at the calloused fingers. The chipped polish. She put her tea down. She took the hand. The grip was warm. Strong. "Glorious mistakes," Riko repeated. She smiled. It felt strange on her face. Unquantized. "I think... I can sequence that." "Good girl," Hana winked, dragging her toward the exit. "Now, about that haggling. Rule one: never look them in the eye until you name your price. Rule two: act like you know where they live..." The automatic doors slid open. The noise of Den Den Town rushed in—traffic, chatter, the distant *pew-pew* of a light gun game, the ozone, the oil. Riko didn't cover her ears. She walked into the static, matching her stride to Hana's, no longer drifting. Moving forward.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and authentic character development within the slice-of-life genre. The author successfully creates two distinct voices through dialogue and internal monologue - Riko's hesitant, technical precision contrasts effectively with Hana's confident, casual directness. The setting of Den Den Town is rendered with sensory detail that feels lived-in rather than researched, from the "ozone, frying oil, and dusty perfume of vintage capacitors" to the specific musical and technical references. The dialogue carries the story effectively, revealing character through speech patterns and shared interests. Riko's technical music knowledge ("measure forty-two," "spectral centroid," "24dB per octave") feels authentic rather than show-offy, while Hana's responses demonstrate genuine appreciation rather than dismissal. The progression from awkward encounter to tentative friendship unfolds naturally through their shared musical obsessions. The prose balances technical specificity with emotional resonance. Musical terminology is woven seamlessly into the narrative voice, suggesting deep subject matter knowledge. The metaphorical language around sound and synthesis ("anxiety was still there... 60-cycle hum. Ground loop") feels organic to Riko's character rather than forced. However, the piece occasionally veers toward over-description, particularly in the opening paragraphs where technical details pile up. Some metaphors feel slightly strained ("carried by the current of the melody"). The transformation from complete social anxiety to collaborative willingness happens quickly, though the shared musical passion provides sufficient motivation. The ending strikes an appropriate note of cautious optimism without overselling the connection. The final image of Riko "no longer drifting. Moving forward" provides closure while maintaining the tentative nature of new friendship. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 63.4
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The box didn’t come from Amazon. It didn’t come from Best Buy. It sat on Leo’s porch in a plain, matte-black cardboard sleeve, no return address, just his name scrawled in Sharpie that looked suspiciously like his own handwriting. Inside, nestled in gray foam, was the **Chronos X**. It wasn’t an Apple Watch. It wasn’t a Fitbit. The band was a weird, iridescent silicone that shifted color like oil on water—purple to green to a bruised yellow. The face was a perfect circle of obsidian glass. No crown. No buttons. Just the screen. Leo, twelve and three-quarters, perpetually late for everything, and currently sporting a cowlick that defied physics and gel, didn't ask questions. He snapped it on. It tightened instantly. Not snug—*fused*. The silicone melted into his wrist hair, warm and pulsing like a second heartbeat. **WELCOME, LEO. TIME REMAINING: 13 YEARS, 244 DAYS, 14 HOURS.** The text flickered in jagged red pixels, burned into the OLED for a split second before vanishing, replaced by a standard digital clock face. 7:42 AM. Leo blinked, rubbing his wrist. "Great. A haunted fitness tracker. Mom’s gonna kill me if it gives me a rash." He trudged to the bus stop, the weight of the watch heavy, not physically, but *gravitationally*. Like it was pulling him toward the center of the earth. He missed the bus. By three seconds. He watched the taillights swallow the stop sign. "Ugh. Come on." He tapped the screen instinctively, frustrated. *Rewind. Just a little.* The air didn't shimmer. There was no *whoosh* sound effect. The universe simply **stuttered**. One second, the bus was turning the corner onto Maple. The next, the brake lights flared red at the stop sign. The doors hissed open. Leo blinked, heart hammering. He scrambled on, flashing his pass. He found a seat behind Jake Miller. *Safe.* He exhaled, slumping against the vinyl. His wrist throbbed. A sharp, hot itch, deep in the radius bone. He scratched it through the band. **TIME REMAINING: 13 YEARS, 244 DAYS, 13 HOURS, 59 MINUTES.** The countdown flickered again. Gone before he could focus. "Whoa, Leo," Jake said, not turning around. "Did you hit a growth spurt overnight? Your shoulders look... wider." Leo frowned. He glanced at his sleeves. The cuffs of his hoodie, usually swallowing his fingertips, now stopped at his wrists. He pulled his hands out. His fingers looked longer. The knuckles sharper. Hair—dark, coarse—dusted the backs of his hands. *Puberty doesn't work that fast,* he thought, a cold spike driving into his gut. *Does it?* At lunch, the cafeteria noise was a physical wall. Leo sat down, tray clattering. His voice dropped an octave when he said, "Pass the ketchup." Sarah Jenkins, who had ignored him since third grade, froze. She looked at him. Really looked. Her eyes traced the line of his jaw—sharper now, shadowed with something that wasn't dirt. She looked at his neck. The Adam’s apple bobbing visibly under the skin. "Leo?" she whispered. "You... you look different. Older." "I feel weird," he admitted, his voice a low rumble in his chest. "My wrist hurts. Bad." He pushed up the sleeve. The Chronos X was *glowing*. A faint, sickly pulse of green light synced with his pulse. **TIME REMAINING: 13 YEARS, 244 DAYS, 10 HOURS.** Ten hours. He’d lost four hours in twenty minutes. "Leo, your face," Sarah said, leaning in, fascinated and repulsed. "Your cheekbones. And your eyes... the corners are crinkled. Like... laugh lines? Or worry lines?" Leo touched his face. The skin felt tighter. Thinner over the bone. He stood up, knocking his bench back. "I have to go. Nurse. Now." He ran. His legs ate up the hallway tile. He was faster. Stronger. His stride lengthened with every step, his inseam stretching the fabric of his jeans until the threads sang. He burst into the bathroom, locking the stall door. He faced the mirror. A stranger stared back. It was him. But it was *him at seventeen*. Maybe eighteen. High cheekbones, jawline cut from granite, stubble darkening his upper lip and chin. The cowlick was gone, replaced by a deliberate, messy sweep of dark hair. The eyes were the same color—hazel—but the whites were shot through with red veins. Tired eyes. Old eyes. "What the hell," the stranger mouthed. The voice was a bass note. **TIME REMAINING: 13 YEARS, 244 DAYS, 9 HOURS, 12 MINUTES.** The watch screamed the numbers at him now. No flicker. Solid red text burned onto the retina. *Every rewind costs time. My time. My future.* He ripped at the band. His fingers—long, strong, veiny—clawed at the iridescent silicone. It didn't budge. It had melted *into* the pores. Part of the circulatory system. He needed to fix this. He needed to undo the bus. Undo the morning. He needed to wake up at 6:00 AM again, twelve years old, with baby fat and a squeaky voice and *time*. He pressed the screen. *Rewind. Rewind it all.* **STUTTER.** The bathroom tiles groaned. The fluorescent lights buzzed backward. The smell of floor wax and Axe body spray reversed into the bottles. He was in his bedroom. Morning light. 6:00 AM sharp. He gasped, scrambling for the mirror on his closet door. *Twelve.* He was twelve. Soft cheeks. High voice. Cowlick standing at attention. Hoodie sleeves swallowing hands. He laughed, a wet, sobbing sound. "It worked. It worked!" He ripped the covers off, ready to dance, ready to kiss the floor— His foot caught the laundry basket. He didn't stumble. He *crashed*. His leg, longer than it should be, tangled in the mesh. His center of gravity, shifted higher by six inches of sudden bone growth, betrayed him. He slammed into the corner of his nightstand. **CRACK.** Pain exploded in his temple. White hot. Blinding. He fell back, the world tilting. Blood, hot and metallic, filled his mouth. He tried to scream for Mom, but the voice that came out was a gurgle. The bedroom door flew open. "Leo? Honey, the bus—" His mom screamed. Not a scared scream. A *wrong* scream. The scream you make when you walk into a room and see a stranger dying on your son's carpet. Because the boy on the floor wasn't twelve. The boy on the floor was twenty-five. Gaunt. Hair thinning at the temples. Deep grooves carved around the mouth and eyes. Hands like claws, spotted with age. A body that had lived three lifetimes in forty minutes. **TIME REMAINING: 0 YEARS, 0 DAYS, 0 HOURS, 0 MINUTES, 10 SECONDS.** The watch face didn't flicker. It burned solid, blinding crimson. **TIME DEBT ACCRUED. PARADOX DETECTED. TIMELINE COLLAPSE IMMINENT.** Leo—*Old Leo*—tried to reach for the watch. His arm wouldn't obey. The nerves had frayed decades ago. His mother backed away, knocking over a lamp. "Who are you? Where is my son? WHERE IS LEO?" "I... am... Leo," he rasped, the vocal cords stiff as leather. "Mom... watch... rewind..." He forced his finger up. One last press. *Please. Just once more. Put it back.* The screen cracked under his fingertip. Spiderwebs of glass. **REWIND INITIATED. FINAL CYCLE.** The world didn't stutter. It *screamed*. The walls of the bedroom peeled away like wallpaper, revealing static. His mother dissolved into pixels. The blood on the carpet un-spilled, flying upward into the gash on his temple. The pain reversed. The years reversed. The bone density softened. The hair thickened. The wrinkles smoothed. **9... 8... 7...** He was falling backward through the years. 20. 18. 16. **6... 5... 4...** He hit the mattress. The impact didn't hurt. He was soft again. Small. **3... 2... 1...** **SYSTEM RESTORED. DEFAULT TIMELINE LOADED.** *** Leo gasped, lungs seizing with the shock of cold air. He was in his bed. The sheets were tangled. The morning light hit the posters on the wall—*Jurassic Park*, a faded soccer schedule. He scrambled up, heart a frantic bird against ribs that were too narrow, too fragile. He ran to the closet mirror. Twelve. Baby fat. Cowlick. Squeaky voice when he yelped, "Mom!" He laughed. Hysterical, high-pitched, *beautiful*. He checked his wrist. Bare skin. Pale, soft, no iridescent band. No scar. Nothing. He sagged against the doorframe, knees weak. "Just a dream. God, just a really messed up dream." "Leo! Bus in five! And bring your laundry down!" "Coming, Mom!" His voice cracked perfectly on the 'o'. He grabbed his backpack, threw on his hoodie. He paused at the door, looking back at the nightstand. A plain, matte-black cardboard sleeve sat there. No return address. His name in Sharpie. *His* handwriting. He froze. The air in the room grew cold. The digital clock on his desk flickered. **7:42 AM.** It didn't say 6:00. It said 7:42. He had slept through the alarm. He had missed the bus. He looked at the box. Then at the clock. Then at his wrist—bare, young, *twelve*. A notification sound chimed from inside the box. A soft, electronic *ping*. Leo’s breath hitched. He hadn't opened it yet. He hadn't put it on. But the countdown had already started. He looked at the closet mirror one last time. Just for a second, the reflection didn't move when he did. The reflection in the mirror *smiled*—a smile with too many teeth, a smile carved by decades of regret—and tapped its wrist. Leo screamed as the bedroom door slammed shut behind him, locking from the *outside*.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, successfully incorporating all required elements: a middle schooler discovering a time-rewinding smartwatch, physical aging consequences, timeline disruption, and the need for one final rewind to fix things. The author captures the appropriate tone for the genre with escalating dread and supernatural elements. The writing shows considerable technical skill in several areas. The imagery is vivid and unsettling - descriptions like "iridescent silicone that shifted color like oil on water" and the watch "fused" to Leo's wrist create effective horror atmosphere. The physical transformation sequences are particularly well-executed, showing Leo's rapid aging through concrete details like lengthening fingers, deepening voice, and changing facial structure. The pacing builds tension effectively, starting with mysterious package delivery and escalating through increasingly disturbing revelations. The concept of time debt and the watch's countdown creates genuine urgency. The author demonstrates good understanding of show-don't-tell principles, revealing Leo's transformation through physical sensations and others' reactions rather than exposition. However, the piece suffers from some significant weaknesses. The dialogue feels stilted and unnatural for middle schoolers - phrases like "Did you hit a growth spurt overnight? Your shoulders look... wider" sound more like adult observations than authentic teen speech. The ending becomes convoluted and overwrought, with multiple reality-bending sequences that strain coherence. The final twist with the reflection and locked door feels forced rather than earned. The prose occasionally veers into purple territory with overwrought descriptions like "universe simply stuttered" and "pain exploded in his temple. White hot. Blinding." Some metaphors feel strained, and the writing sometimes prioritizes style over clarity. Character development is limited - Leo remains fairly one-dimensional throughout, reacting to events rather than driving them. His mother's brief appearance lacks authenticity. The emotional complexity is surface-level, focusing more on horror beats than deeper psychological exploration. The piece succeeds as genre fiction but lacks the subtlety and earned emotional weight that would elevate it beyond competent pastiche. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Cyclone screamed its rusted lullaby, a shriek of metal and momentum that vibrated in the fillings of her teeth. Clara pressed her gloved fingertips against the splintered railing of the boardwalk, the salt wind whipping the hem of her navy wool coat around her calves. It was July, sticky and thick, but she hadn't removed the coat. She hadn't removed the gloves. Armor, both of them. **His locks.** The phrase rose again, unbidden, tasting of pomade and something older. *Locks*. Not hair. Not curls. A word from a Brontë novel or a penny dreadful, the kind her mother burned in the furnace. It implied possession. It implied a hand tangled deep, pulling. She inhaled sharply through her nose. Cotton candy. Burnt sugar and vanilla, cloying and chemical, drifting from a cart three stalls down. *County fair. 1922. Iowa, maybe. Or Ohio.* A sticky finger tracing a line down a chubby cheek. A man’s voice, low and laughing, *Here, princess, eat it before it melts into your ribs.* The memory had no face. Just the smell, and the terrifying lightness of the confection dissolving on her tongue—sweetness vanishing the moment you tried to hold it. " You’re shivering." The voice came from the shadows behind the shooting gallery counter, where the barker had folded his canvas and gone to supper. Clara didn’t jump. She had felt him before she heard him—the displacement of air, the sudden drop in temperature that had nothing to do with the ocean. She turned. He leaned against the support beam, a cigarette burning between two long fingers. The carnival lights—bare bulbs strung on sagging wire—caught the obsidian wave of his hair, the sharp architecture of his jaw. He wore a charcoal suit, impeccably cut, the kind that whispered *money* in a place that smelled of fryer grease and rust. He looked like a mistake she had already decided to make. "I’m not shivering," she said. Her voice was steady. She was proud of that. "The wind off the Atlantic carries a bite." "Does it?" He pushed off the beam. He moved with a liquid economy, a predator disguised as a gentleman. He stopped an inch too close. The scent of him cut through the salt and sugar: tobacco, rain on hot asphalt, and something dark, floral. Night-blooming jasmine, perhaps. Or poison. "You’re wearing wool in July, Clara. You’re either ill, or you’re waiting for someone to peel it off you." The use of her name was a physical blow. She had never given it to him. Not last week in the automat on 42nd Street, not two nights ago in the back booth of the jazz cellar in Harlem. She had given him *Miss*, and *Madam*, and once, breathlessly, *Don't*. "How do you know my name?" The question was a whisper. He smiled. It didn't reach his eyes. They were pupils swallowed by iris, bottomless. "I asked the woman at the flower stand on Surf Avenue. The one who sells gardenias. She remembers the lady in the navy coat who buys a single bloom every Tuesday and throws it in the trash can on the corner before the train." Clara’s throat clicked. "I don't—" "Don't lie to me." The command was soft, edged with velvet. "It insults the both of us. You throw them away because you don't deserve them. That’s the story you tell yourself. But you keep buying them. That’s the truth." **He sees the fracture. He names it. He owns it.** The thought was treacherous. She clenched her gloved hands at her sides. "You have a remarkable talent for turning observation into insult." "Insult?" He laughed, a low rumble. "I call it appetite. You’re starving, Clara. You’ve been starving since Iowa. Since the man with the sticky fingers and the gardenias stopped coming home." The air left her lungs. The cotton candy smell gagged her, sudden and violent. *Princess. Eat it before it melts.* Her father. The gardenias were for his grave. She bought them because she couldn't bear the weight of the stone, and she threw them away because she couldn't bear the weight of the grief. "You know nothing," she hissed, the composure cracking, just a hairline fracture. "I know you came back." He reached out. She flinched. He didn't touch her—just let his fingers hover over the lapel of her coat, the wool rough against the silk of his pocket square. "You promised you wouldn't. You said, *This is the last time, I am a respectable woman, I have a fiancé in Albany who sells dry goods.*" "I do have a fiancé," she said. The lie tasted like ash. "Arthur. He sells textiles." "Arthur," he repeated, tasting the name like spoiled wine. "Does Arthur know you wear another man’s initials on your lingerie? The silk camisole. Blue. *J.L.* stitched at the hem." Clara’s hand flew to her throat, her fingers finding the high collar of her blouse. **How? When?** "You were asleep," he murmured, answering the silent question. "The night at the Waldorf. Three weeks ago. I didn't take them. I just looked. I memorized the stitching. *J.L.* Julian LeClerc. My tailor. My initials. On your skin." **He didn't take them. He just looked. That is somehow far worse.** "You’re a monster," she breathed. "I’m a man who keeps his word." He finally bridged the gap. His knuckles grazed the wool of her shoulder, a whisper of contact that burned through the fabric, branding the skin beneath. "I told you I’d be here at dusk. I told you I’d give you a reason to stay. Or a reason to run. You chose to stand still." "Because I wanted to see if you were real," she lied. The truth was a live wire in her mouth: *I wanted to see if I would burn.* "Real enough to know you hate the cotton candy," he said. His thumb traced the line of her jaw, tilting her chin up. "Real enough to know you taste like gin and regret. Real enough to know that when I kiss you, you’re going to open your mouth for me before your brain catches up to your body." The arrogance should have repulsed her. It should have sent her marching back to the BMT platform, back to Arthur and the textiles and the quiet, airless life of a respectable wife. **Open your mouth. Let him in. Let him ruin the carpet.** "Julian," she whispered. The name felt foreign. Dangerous. A key turning in a lock she had welded shut. "Say it again," he commanded. "Say it like you mean it. Like you’re not thinking of Albany." She looked at the shooting gallery behind him. The painted ducks and bears, frozen in perpetual flight. Cheap targets for men with bad aim and something to prove. She felt like one of them—painted wood, waiting for the pellet. "I don't know what I mean," she admitted. The honesty surprised her. "I only know that when I smell burnt sugar, I see a grave. And when I look at you, I don't see a future. I see the shovel." Julian didn't flinch. His smile sharpened, becoming something hungry and honest. "Good. Then we understand each other. I’m not the future, Clara. I’m the wreckage. The question is whether you want to drown in the wreckage, or die of thirst on the shore." He leaned down, his lips brushing the shell of her ear. The cigarette smoke curled around them, a private fog. "Put the gun down," he whispered. "You don't need to win the bear. You just need to decide if you're brave enough to lose yourself." His hand found the first button of her coat. Metal teeth, parting. Clara didn't stop him. She didn't step back. She stared at the flashing lights of the Wonder Wheel, turning slow and inevitable against the bruising purple sky, and she exhaled a breath she had been holding since 1922. "Unbutton it," she said. Her voice didn't tremble. "But if you tear the fabric, LeClerc, you’re buying me a new coat." His laugh was a dark thing, vibrating against her cheek as his mouth found the pulse hammering in her neck. "Darling. I’ll buy you the whole damn boardwalk. Just let me watch you burn."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested atmosphere of romantic danger with restrained sensuality. The author successfully captures the 1930s Coney Island setting through vivid sensory details - the rusted Cyclone, salt wind, cotton candy aromas, and carnival lights create an immersive backdrop that feels authentic to the era. The characterization is particularly strong. Clara emerges as a complex figure haunted by childhood trauma (the father with "sticky fingers" and gardenias), trapped between respectability and desire. Her internal contradictions - buying flowers for her father's grave then throwing them away, wearing another man's initials on her lingerie while claiming to have a fiancé - create psychological depth. Julian is effectively portrayed as a predatory yet magnetic figure who sees through her defenses with unsettling precision. The dialogue crackles with tension and subtext. Lines like "You're either ill, or you're waiting for someone to peel it off you" and "I'm not the future, Clara. I'm the wreckage" establish character dynamics efficiently while maintaining the requested edge. The power play between them feels authentic - his dominance through observation and psychological manipulation, her resistance gradually crumbling. The prose style successfully balances literary sophistication with accessibility. Phrases like "liquid economy, a predator disguised as a gentleman" and "appetite disguised as observation" demonstrate elegant word choice without becoming overwrought. The author effectively uses sensory details and metaphors (Clara feeling like a painted duck target) to externalize internal states. The piece adheres well to the structural requirements - roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from Clara's nervous anticipation to Julian's psychological dominance to her final capitulation. The ending feels earned rather than rushed, as we've witnessed her defenses systematically dismantled. However, these are minor quibbles in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while demonstrating genuine literary merit. Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.

The guide's name was Obediah, though everyone called him Obie, and usually you couldn't shut him up. JT had known the man since he was knee-high to a snowmobile, a fixture of these autumns as reliable as the first hard frost. Obie talked through breakfast, talked on the trail, talked over cards and cheap whiskey deep into the night—stories about the logging days, about the winter of '78 when the snow buried the first floor, about the tourist from Connecticut who'd wandered off trail and turned up three weeks later in a stand of tamarack, frozen solid but smiling, they said, smiling like he'd found God in the dark. Obie talked, and JT's father listened with the patient tolerance of a man who'd heard it all before, and Mike laughed at the right spots, and JT just watched the way the firelight moved across Obie's face, the deep lines around his mouth, the tobacco-stained fingers gesturing wide. This year, Obie hadn't said ten words since they'd arrived. He moved through the lodge like a ghost in his own house, shoulders hunched, eyes darting to the windows with a frequency that looked almost compulsive. He cooked in silence—venison stew, dense bannock, coffee strong enough to stand a spoon in—and when JT's father tried to joke about the election, about the price of ammunition, about the new ranger station going up down at the highway turnoff, Obie just nodded, jaw tight, and walked out the back door without a word. The third night, JT found him on the porch. The moon was a sliver, barely a thumbnail paring in the black, but the snow drank what little light existed and threw it back up, rendering the tree line in shades of charcoal and bone. Obie sat in the rocking chair, a blanket across his knees despite the woodstove's warmth bleeding through the walls. He held a rifle across his lap—not one of the hunting pieces, JT noticed. Something older. The stock was worn smooth as river stone, the barrel blued nearly black. "Obie?" JT said, stepping onto the boards. They didn't creak. Nothing creaked anymore. "You alright?" The old man's head turned slow. His eyes, in the dimness, looked entirely pupil. No white showing at all. "Go to bed, boy." "Just—" JT stopped. The cold bit through his thermal socks. "You've been quiet. All week. Dad's wondering. Mike's wondering. I'm wondering." A sound escaped Obie's throat. Might have been a laugh, might have been a cough. "Your daddy don't wonder about nothin' real. Your brother neither. They see what they expect to see. Always have." "And what's that supposed to mean?" Obie's gaze drifted past JT's shoulder, toward the woods. "Means the season's wrong. Means the caribou don't run right. Means the woods are full of things that ain't caribou, and you're the only one with sense enough to be scared." JT's pulse kicked. "I'm not scared. I'm just—tired. Cold. It's been a long drive." "Uh-huh." The old man's fingers tightened on the rifle stock. "You saw the buck in the clearing. Three days ago. Don't lie to me, boy. I know that look. Seen it in the mirror often enough." JT's throat clicked. "I don't know what you're talking about." "Course you don't. Knowing's the problem. Not knowing's the mercy." Obie rocked once, twice. The chair didn't squeak. "Full moon's in four nights. You need to be gone before then. All of you. Pack up tomorrow. Tell your daddy the weather's turning. Tell him whatever you need to tell him. But you get out." "The weather's fine. Clear and cold. Perfect hunting." "Hunting." Obie spat off the porch, a dark glob on the snow. "You think that's what this is? You think any of this is hunting?" The question hung between them, vast and cold as the valley below. Somewhere in the trees, something moved—branch against branch, or maybe something heavier. JT's hand found the porch post, splintered wood biting his palm. "What happens at the full moon?" he asked, quiet. Obie didn't answer. Just stared into the tree line, and JT followed his gaze, and for a moment—just a heartbeat—he thought he saw eyes reflecting back. Not deer eyes. Too high. Too wide. The wrong color entirely, a pale yellow-green like sick moss. "Go to bed," Obie said again, softer now. "And JT? Don't walk alone at night. Not even to the shitter. Especially not then." --- The dream came again that night, same as the past three nights. JT stood in the clearing. The buck stood before him, massive and patient, breath pluming in air that didn't feel cold. His father's hand hovered near the animal's muzzle, trembling. Mike stood shoulder-to-shoulder with him, both men motionless as statues, both wearing that expression—hungry, reverent, *empty*. JT wanted to scream. His throat wouldn't work. His legs wouldn't move. The buck turned its head. Looked directly at him. Its eyes were human. Brown. Familiar. His mother's eyes, gone twelve years now, cancer taking her slow in a hospital room that smelled of antiseptic and regret. She'd loved these trips. Loved the lodge, the silence, the way the stars looked like they'd been scattered by a careless hand. She'd died in July, and his father had brought them north that October anyway, said the season waited for no one, said she'd have wanted them to go. The buck opened its mouth, and his mother's voice came out: *Jonathan. You're late for supper.* He woke gasping, heart hammering, sheets soaked through. The lodge was silent. No snoring from Mike's bunk. No creak of floorboards from his father's room down the hall. Just silence, thick and watchful. JT sat up slowly. The window showed the moon, fatter now, two nights fuller. Light spilled across the floorboards in a pale rectangle. He counted his breaths. One. Two. Three. A floorboard creaked. Downstairs. Heavy, deliberate. Then another. And another. Coming up the stairs. JT's hand found the flashlight under his pillow. His father's .30-06 leaned in the corner, but the bolt was open, shells in the box on the shelf—safety first, always safety first, *Jonathan, you treat every gun like it's loaded, you hear me?*—and there wasn't time. The footsteps stopped outside his door. A knock. Three raps. Polite. "JT?" His father's voice. Muffled through the wood. "You awake, son?" JT exhaled, body sagging. "Yeah. Yeah, Dad. What is it?" "Mike's gone. Been gone a while, looks like. His bed's cold. Boots missing. Rifle too." The flashlight beam trembled in JT's grip. "He probably just went out early. First light. You know Mike." "First light's two hours off. And he didn't leave a note. Your brother don't *do* notes, I know, but..." A pause. A breath. "There's tracks. Leading out back. Toward the clearing." JT was already moving, pulling on boots, grabbing his jacket. "I'll go get him. He's probably just—" "Stay here." The command stopped him cold. His father *never* used that tone. Not with him. Not since he was ten and wandered too close to the river during spring runoff. "Dad—" "I said stay here, Jonathan. I'm not asking. Obie's already out there. He went quiet, ten minutes past. Didn't wake me. Didn't wake anyone. Just... went." The doorknob turned. His father's face appeared in the gap, pale in the moonlight spilling from the hallway window. The man looked older than JT had ever seen him, lines carved deep around eyes that held the same flat brightness JT had watched in the clearing three days ago. "Lock this door," his father said. "Don't open it for nobody. Not even me. You hear me? Not even me." The door closed. Footsteps receded. Heavy. Fast. JT stood in the center of his room, flashlight beam dancing across walls papered with decades of hunting permits, yellowed photos, a mounted trout that had never looked quite right—mouth too wide, eyes too blank. *Lock this door. Don't open it for nobody. Not even me.* His fingers found the deadbolt. Threw it home. The *clack* sounded final. Loud in the quiet. He moved to the window. The clearing was visible from here, a pale wound in the dark forest. He could see shapes moving—two, maybe three—converging on the space where the buck had stood. One moved wrong. Loping. Too low to the ground. Obie. His father. And the third— The third stood upright. Stood *still*. Even at this distance, JT knew the posture. The set of the shoulders. The way the head tilted, listening. Mike. The moon chose that moment to break through a thin scud of cloud, silvering the clearing fully. And JT saw the thing standing beside his brother. It wasn't a caribou. It stood on two legs. Tall. Impossibly tall, seven feet at least, elongated limbs folded against a torso that seemed to shift and blur at the edges. Antlers—*branches*, really, crowned with velvet—rose from a skull that had no face. Just smooth bone where features should be, catching the moonlight like polished ivory. Mike reached up. Touched the thing's chest. A gesture of worship. Of recognition. And the thing *bowed its head*. JT's breath fogged the glass. His reflection superimposed over the scene—pale face, wide eyes, mouth open on a silent no no no no— The thing's head snapped up. No eyes. No face. Just smooth bone. But JT felt it looking at him. Felt it *know* him. *Jonathan. You're late for supper.* The flashlight slipped from numb fingers. Clattered on the floorboards. Behind him, the doorknob turned. Slow. Deliberate. The deadbolt held. Something scratched at the wood. Long, slow strokes. *Scritch. Scritch. Scritch.* A voice whispered through the grain—his father's voice, but wrong. Flattened. Stretched thin over something else. *"Open up, son. We got one. Biggest buck you ever saw. Come see. Come touch."* JT backed away, heels hitting the bed frame. The scratching stopped. The voice changed. Became Mike's. Bright. Excited. *Wrong.* *"JT! You gotta see this. It's not what we thought. It's so much better. It's been waiting for us. Waiting for YOU."* A third voice. Older. Raspier. Obie's. *"Boy, you listen to me. You keep that door shut. You keep it shut till morning. Whatever you hear. Whatever you see. It ain't us. It ain't never been us."* The three voices spoke at once, a chorus of familiar tones saying *come out come out come out we're family we're blood we're the season—* JT clamped his hands over his ears. Slid down the bed frame to the floor. Pulled his knees tight. Squeezed his eyes shut. *Not real. Not real. Dream. Still dreaming. Wake up. Wake up.* The doorknob rattled. The frame shuddered under weight. And somewhere, distantly, a rifle cracked. Once. Twice. Then silence fell so complete it rang in his ears. The moon, he realized dimly, was full now. Perfectly, terribly full. And the scratching at his door began again.

+ Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 88.2
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Model Output:
The screaming started at 6:00 AM, which was reasonable. The screaming *stopped* at 6:03 AM, which was a personnel issue. Lucifer Morningstar, Lightbringer, Lord of the Flies, and CEO of Gehenna Holdings LLC, sighed into his artisanal cold brew. The coffee was made from beans grown in the ashen soil of the Seventh Circle, roasted over the burning ambition of fallen CEOs, and brewed by a hydrocephalic imp named Kevin. It tasted like regret and dark chocolate notes. "Kevin," Lucifer said, not looking up from the quarterly damnation projections. "The screaming. It lacks *sustain*." Kevin trembled, his three eyes watering. "Sir, the new intake from the 'Corporate Synergy' sector—well, their vocal cords gave out. We’re waiting on replacements from the 'Reality TV Producers' batch. They have remarkable lung capacity, sir. Generations of practice." "Expedite it," Lucifer said. "Silence in Hell implies contentment. Contentment implies hope. Hope is a paperwork nightmare." He tapped his fountain pen (inked with the blood of a martyr who died for a typo) against the desk. The office was vast, carved from a single stalactite of obsidian, furnished with the skins of beasts that didn't make the Ark. But today, the grandeur felt drafty. The heavy oak doors—salvaged from the Garden of Eden’s east gate, still smelling faintly of fig and divine wrath—didn't open. They *dissolved* into a cloud of sulfur and expensive perfume. Lilith walked in. She wore a trench coat the color of a bruised plum, lined with the fur of the last Siberian Unicorn. Her hair, a cascade of midnight unconcerned with gravity, framed a face that had launched a thousand ships, sunk two continents, and once convinced a Seraph to trade his wings for a motorcycle. She carried the purse. The purse was a scorched leather satchel, stitched with thread spun from the beards of drowned philosophers. It smelled of ozone, old library books, and the distinct, metallic tang of a mortal soul that hadn't quite finished dying. "Lucy," she said. Her voice was honey poured over broken glass. "You’re brooding. It ruins the complexion. And the upholstery." "I don't brood, Lilith," Lucifer said, capping the pen. "I conduct strategic melancholy. There’s a difference. One is tax-deductible." "Mm." She drifted toward the wet bar, which was actually a fissure in reality dispensing single-malt scotch aged in the skulls of corrupt popes. "You’re out of the good stuff. The 14th Century vintage. I can taste the simony from here." "Budget cuts. The War in Heaven’s pension fund is bleeding us dry. Michael keeps submitting expense reports for 'flaming sword maintenance.' It’s a prop, Michael. It runs on drama, not gasoline." She poured two fingers anyway, the liquid catching the non-light of the non-windows. She didn't sit. She perched on the edge of the chair made from the ribcage of Leviathan, crossing legs that had walked the dust before God said "Let there be." "So," she said. "The screaming." "Personnel shortage. Kevin is incompetent." "Kevin has three heads and a nervous tic. You promoted him because he remembered how you take your coffee." "He remembers *how* I take it. He forgets *that* I take it. The distinction is the difference between a loyal servant and a statistic." Lilith smiled. It was a dangerous thing, sharp and rare. She reached into the scorched purse. The inside of the bag was a violation of physics. It went deep—*deep*—past the lining, past the seams, into a pocket dimension where lost socks and forgotten promises went to ferment. Her arm disappeared to the shoulder. She rummaged past a dried pomegranate seed (the original), a vial of the Black Death (vintage 1347, very dry), a smartphone cracked but still playing *Candy Crush* (soul of a teenager, infinite lives), and a single, perfect human molar (gold filling, molar #19, lower left). "Ah," she whispered. She pulled out a small, plastic container. Tupperware. Pale blue lid, slightly warped. "I brought lunch," she said. Lucifer stared at the Tupperware. "Is that... lasagna?" "Spinach and ricotta. No meat. Friday abstinence, technically, though the calendar down here is more of a suggestion." She set it on the desk, next to the damnation projections. "I stole the recipe from a grandmother in Bologna. She died of a heart attack stirring the pot. Irony improves the flavor." "You brought me leftovers. In Tupperware. From a dead Italian woman." "I brought you *sustenance*, Lucifer. You forget to eat. You forget to sleep. You forget that you’re not a concept, you’re a person. A very tall, very dramatic person with daddy issues and a vitamin D deficiency." "I am the Adversary. I do not require vitamins. I require obedience." "Obedience doesn't stop the shaking in your left hand when the caffeine wears off." She snapped the lid off. The smell hit him—basil, tomato, garlic, butter. It smelled like a Tuesday afternoon in a kitchen with a checkered tablecloth. It smelled like *mercy*. It was the most offensive thing he had smelled in six thousand years. "You're doing it again," he said, voice low. "Doing what?" "Domesticity. It’s a trap. It’s how they get you. First it’s lasagna, next it’s throw pillows, then you’re arguing about whose turn it is to walk the Cerberus and I am *not* picking up the droppings of a three-headed dog the size of a mountain range." "Cerberus is house-trained. Mostly. He prefers the Styx." She conjured a fork from the air—silver, engraved with *Property of the Inquisition, Toledo Branch*. "Eat. The projections can wait. The damned have waited centuries. Another hour won't damper their enthusiasm." He looked at the fork. He looked at the lasagna. He looked at her—really looked. The bags under her eyes (immortality doesn't cure insomnia). The chipped nail polish on her thumb (black, chipped from prying open the Gates of Dis). The way she held the fork loosely, ready to weaponize it, or defend him. The loneliness wasn't a void. It was a heavy, wet blanket. And she was the only thing sharp enough to cut it. "Fine," Lucifer muttered. He took the fork. "But if this is a poison plot, it’s derivative. I invented arsenic." "It's gluten-free," she said. "The wheat in the Ninth Circle causes bloating." He took a bite. It was perfect. The cheese pulled in strings that defied thermodynamics. The pasta had the *al dente* resistance of a soul clinging to a lie. It tasted like forgiveness, which is the spiciest flavor in Hell. "Good," he admitted, mouth full. "The ricotta has a certain... *je ne sais quoi*. Is that despair?" "Nutmeg," she corrected. "And a pinch of 'Unrequited Longing.' I harvested it from a poet in the Wood of the Suicides. Very aromatic." They ate in silence. The screaming outside had resumed—Kevin had clearly secured the Reality TV batch—but in here, there was only the clink of silver on plastic. Lucifer wiped his mouth with a napkin woven from the Shroud of Turin (a forgery, but a good one). "You've been stopping by. Tuesdays. Thursdays. Last week you fixed the thermostat in the Pit of Flattery. The week before, you reorganized the Library of Lies. Dewey Decimal is a tool of oppression, by the way. You alphabetized by *victim*." "I was bored," Lilith said, packing the empty Tupperware back into the infinite purse. "The mortal realm is tedious. They’ve automated sin. There’s no artistry left. No *passion*. They just doom-scroll into the abyss. Where’s the craft? Where’s the temptation?" "You miss the work." "I miss the *chaos*, Lucy. Order is your department. I’m the entropy." She stood up, the plum coat swirling. "I have a meeting in the City of Dis. A negotiation with the Furies. They want dental. I have to explain that teeth are a luxury for the living." "Stay," he said. The word hung in the air, heavier than the obsidian desk, heavier than the Crown of Thorns he kept in a drawer for headaches. Lilith paused. Her hand rested on the doorknob (a human femur, polished smooth). She didn't turn around. "Lucifer," she said, soft as the fall of snow on a grave. "We don't 'stay.' We collide. We orbit. We burn. 'Stay' implies a future. We have eternity. Eternity doesn't have a future. It only has *now*." "Then stay for *now*," he said. "The lasagna was good. The coffee is terrible. Kevin is screaming about a union grievance. I have a headache the size of the Lake of Fire. Stay. Help me fire Kevin. Help me deny the Furies dental. Help me be... this. Whatever this is." She was silent for a long moment. The only sound was the scratching of his pen on the damnation ledger—*Denied. Denied. Approved (ironic punishment). Denied.* Slowly, she turned. The danger in her face had softened into something terrifyingly tender. She walked back to the desk, reached into the purse one last time, and pulled out a small, white bottle. "Aspirin," she said, setting it down. "Bayer. Stolen from a pharmacy in 1918. Still potent. Take two. Drink water. Not scotch. Water." "Water is for the baptized." "Water is for the dehydrated. Drink it." She leaned down, pressing a kiss to his forehead. It tasted of sulfur, pomegranates, and the cold vacuum of space. "Same time tomorrow?" she asked, straightening up. "Bring the cannoli," he said. "The ones from the bakery in Little Italy. The baker sells his soul every Tuesday for a good review in the Times. I want the ricotta filling." "Deal." She smiled, a real one, small and private. "Don't let Kevin unionize. It sets a precedent. The imps in Accounting are already talking about a 401k." "Out," he said, waving a hand. "Go tempt the Furies. Tell them flossing is a mortal sin." "Liar." "Expert." She dissolved back into sulfur and perfume. The doors reassembled themselves with a sound like a tomb closing. Lucifer Morningstar, Prince of Darkness, Father of Lies, sat alone in his office carved from the bone of the world. He opened the aspirin bottle. Shook two white pills into his palm. Swallowed them dry. He picked up the pen, dipped it in the martyr's blood, and wrote at the top of the next page: *Personnel Review: Kevin. Outcome: Promoted to Middle Management (Eternal).* Then he opened the bottom drawer, pulled out a throw pillow embroidered with *HOME IS WHERE THE HEART IS (RIPPED OUT)*, and placed it carefully behind his lower back. It helped. He began to work.
