+ Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 77.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7482 **Object Class:** Thaumiel (Pending Reclassification: Archon) **Special Containment Procedures:** All instances of SCP-7482-A are to be sealed with reinforced concrete and monitored by embedded Foundation assets in local law enforcement. Mobile Task Force Eta-10 ("See No Evil") maintains a permanent presence at Site-7482, established within the primary manifestation beneath the ruins of the Buzludzha Monument, Bulgaria. Exploration of SCP-7482-B requires O5 authorization. Following Incident 7482-Ω, all personnel entering SCP-7482-B are equipped with temporal displacement monitors and prohibited from accessing any document dated prior to 1900 CE without direct Overseer approval. No fewer than three members of the O5 Council must be present for any review of materials recovered from Sector 9. **Description:** SCP-7482 refers to a phenomenon involving the spontaneous manifestation of identical doors (designated SCP-7482-A) within abandoned or condemned structures worldwide. To date, 1,742 instances have been documented across 84 countries. Each SCP-7482-A instance is a single-leaf door, 2.1m × 0.9m, constructed of an unidentified composite material resembling aged oak but possessing a tensile strength exceeding 400 MPa. No manufacturer markings, hinges, or locking mechanisms are present. The doors are uniformly unmarked save for a single engraved symbol on the upper-left panel: a circle bisected by a vertical line, flanked by two dots—consistent with the logo of the **Vindex Institute**, an organization with no historical record. Notably, multiple SCP-7482-A instances exhibit weathering patterns inconsistent with their host structures. Radiocarbon dating of surface patina on Instance 7482-A-44 (manifested in a 1970s Detroit housing project) returned a date of 11,200 ± 150 years BP. The building was constructed in 1972. All SCP-7482-A instances open into SCP-7482-B: a single, non-Euclidean archival complex of indeterminate size. Spatial mapping via drone telemetry and GPS relay has failed; laser rangefinders return contradictory distances, and inertial navigation systems drift by up to 400% within minutes of entry. The architecture incorporates materials and engineering principles unknown to modern science—load-bearing columns of transparent ceramic, vaulted ceilings supported by tension fields rather than compression, and corridors that appear to fold through themselves without intersection. SCP-7482-B contains an estimated 10^8 to 10^12 discrete documents, stored on media ranging from fired clay tablets to crystalline data lattices. All recovered materials reference a global civilization designated **"The Axiom"** (translated from the recurring term *Axíōma*), which achieved planetary unification approximately 12,000 years ago. The Axiom maintained a centralized anomaly containment infrastructure referred to as **The Vault**. According to recovered texts, The Axiom was destroyed by a **Class-Zero Containment Failure**—an event in which a single uncontained entity (designated *Subject Prime*) breached The Vault's central repository, triggering a cascading collapse of reality stabilization systems. The resulting "Unmaking" erased The Axiom from history, leaving no archaeological trace. --- ### **Addendum 7482.1: Recovered Document Excerpts** **Document 7482-001** — *Clay Tablet, Sector 3, Row 11, Shelf 400* > **VAULT DIRECTIVE 991-ALPHA** > **CLASSIFICATION: PRIME / EYES ONLY** > > Subject Prime is not an anomaly. It is the *consequence* of containment. Every entity we secure, every reality we stabilize, every law we enforce upon the chaotic—each act of binding generates an equal and opposite potential for rupture. We have contained 14,000 anomalies. The debt is due. > > The Unmaking cannot be stopped. It can only be *survived*. > > Begin Protocol **ARCHIVE**. Preserve all knowledge. Preserve the *institution*. When the dust settles, the work resumes. > > — **Director Valerius, Vault Prime** > *Stardate 12,043.7 (correlates to ~10,000 BCE)* **Document 7482-002** — *Crystalline Lattice, Sector 7, Core Spire* > **PERSONNEL FILE: DR. ELIAS VAUGHN** > **CLEARANCE: LEVEL 5 / OVERSEER CANDIDATE** > **DOB:** 1847-03-14 | **DOD:** [REDACTED] > **ASSIGNMENT:** Vault Prime, Department of Ontological Stability > **NOTES:** Subject displays anomalous temporal fixation. Retains memories of timelines nullified by Class-IV reality restructuring events. Recommended for Overseer elevation pending loyalty verification. > **CURRENT STATUS:** **ACTIVE** — *See Addendum 7482.4* **Document 7482-003** — *Polymer Film, Sector 12, Annex C* > **INSTITUTIONAL CHARTER — VINDEX INSTITUTE** > **ARTICLE I: PURPOSE** > The Vindex Institute shall endure beyond the death of nations, the fall of empires, and the erasure of history. We are the constant. We secure. We contain. We protect. > > **ARTICLE VII: SUCCESSION** > In the event of civilizational collapse, the Institute shall reconstitute under whatever nomenclature the surviving populace adopts. The symbol (⦿) shall persist. The mission shall persist. The *personnel* shall persist. > > **SIGNATORIES:** Valerius, Keres, Thorne, **O5-1**, **O5-2**, **O5-3**, [REDACTED], [REDACTED], [REDACTED], **O5-13** --- ### **Addendum 7482.2: Exploration Log 7482-04** **Team:** MTF Eta-10 ("See No Evil") — 6 personnel **Objective:** Penetrate Sector 9 (designated "The Overseer Wing" per recovered indices) **Date:** 2024-03-14 **[BEGIN LOG]** **00:00** — Team enters SCP-7482-B via Instance 7482-A-1 (Buzludzha Monument). Spatial distortion negligible at entry threshold. Drone relay active. **01:22** — Team reaches Sector 3. Architecture shifts: corridors widen, lighting transitions from bioluminescent panels to directed hard-light projectors. Document density increases by ~300%. **03:47** — **Contact.** Thermal imaging detects twelve humanoid signatures 200m ahead, moving through a junction into Sector 9. Entities wear full-body sealed suits resembling Foundation-standard hazardous environment gear (Model 1983), but lacking insignia. Each carries a modular apparatus connected to the walls via umbilicals—apparatuses actively *extracting* shelving units, document racks, and entire wall sections into portable containment frames. **04:11** — Team advances. Entities cease extraction. Helmets rotate 180° in unison. No facial features visible through visors. **04:13** — **Entity Vocalization** (via external speaker): > *"Unauthorized presence in Sector 9. Withdraw immediately. Authorization code required."* **04:15** — Team Leader (Captain Aris Thorne) responds with Foundation challenge phrase: *"In darkness, we are the light."* **04:16** — Entities freeze. Apparatuses disengage from walls with audible *thunk*. All twelve entities retreat at high speed—estimated 40 km/h—*backwards*, maintaining visual contact. They do not turn. They vanish into a side corridor that did not exist moments prior. Spatial mapping shows the corridor terminates in a dead end 15m in. Entities not recovered. **04:22** — Team enters Sector 9. Extraction frames abandoned mid-operation. Contents include: - 3,400 personnel files (all Foundation staff, past and present) - 17 O5 Council meeting transcripts dated 2025–2031 (future-dated) - 1 architectural schematic of Site-01 labeled **"REVISION 14 — POST-UNMAKING"** - 1 sealed cylinder containing a living human finger (DNA match: **O5-7**, sampled 2024-01-12) **05:03** — Team discovers a desk at Sector 9 centroid. Surface bears a single document: a handwritten note on Foundation letterhead (watermark: *SCP Foundation — Est. 1892*). > *Thorne—* > > *You weren't supposed to find this. None of you were. The Archive removes what the Council cannot risk you knowing. We've been coming here for decades. Every Overseer since 1924. We take what we need. We burn what we don't.* > > *Subject Prime is not in the past. It's in the basement of Site-01. It's the thing we built the Foundation to contain. And it's waking up.* > > *Don't trust the symbol. Don't trust the Institute. And for God's sake, don't let them finish the extraction.* > > *– **O5-1** (The One Who Remembers)* **05:07** — Temporal displacement monitors on all team members spike: **+12,000 years / -0 seconds**. Local reality index drops to 0.12. **05:08** — **Extraction Complete.** Sector 9 *ceases to exist*. Corridor terminates in a blank wall of the composite door-material. No trace of extracted materials, entities, or the desk. **05:10** — Team extracts. Debrief pending. **[END LOG]** --- ### **Addendum 7482.3: Incident 7482-Ω** On 2024-03-18, routine surveillance of O5 Council communications (authorized under Emergency Protocol 000-Omega) intercepted a transmission from **O5-1** to **O5-13**: > *The Archive knows. The extraction teams failed to clean Sector 9 in time. Eta-10 saw the finger. They saw the transcripts. They saw my note.* > > *Convene the Council. Full disclosure. We are not the first Foundation. We are the *latest iteration*. And if we don't stop the extraction, there won't be a next one.* The O5 Council convened at Site-01 on 2024-03-19. **O5-1 through O5-13 attended. O5-14 was absent.** **O5-14's personnel file, recovered from Sector 9 extraction frame #7, lists a date of death: 2024-03-18. Cause of death: "Removal by Vindex Institute — Unauthorized Knowledge Retention."** **O5-14 is currently alive and serving at Site-01. No medical anomalies detected.** --- ### **Addendum 7482.4: Note on Dr. Elias Vaughn** Dr. Elias Vaughn is currently employed as a Senior Researcher at Site-19, specializing in temporal anomalies. He was born in 1982. He has no record of Overseer candidacy. When presented with Document 7482-002, Dr. Vaughn suffered a catastrophic cerebrovascular event. During the 4 minutes 13 seconds of clinical death, he was recorded speaking fluent **Axiom High Dialect** (previously unattested in any Foundation linguistic database). Translation of his vocalizations: > *"The debt is paid. The cycle turns. Valerius lies. The Unmaking was not a failure. It was a **harvest**. And the Institute... the Institute is the **farmer**."* Dr. Vaughn revived spontaneously with no neurological damage. He retains no memory of the event. His personnel file has since been flagged by the Foundation's automated records system with a single new entry, added **by an unknown user at 03:14:00 on 2024-03-19**: > **STATUS UPDATE: OVERSEER CANDIDATE VAUGHN — LOYALTY VERIFICATION PENDING. RECOMMENDATION: ACCELERATED.** The user ID matches **O5-1's** credentials. O5-1 denies making the entry. --- **Footnotes:** 1. The symbol ⦿ appears on all SCP-7482-A instances, all Vindex Institute documents, and the cornerstone of Site-01 (laid 1924). 2. Radiocarbon dating of the Site-01 cornerstone returns a date of **10,200 BCE**. 3. Subject Prime remains unidentified. Cross-referencing with SCP-001 proposals is **strictly prohibited** by order of the O5 Council (Vote: 12-1, O5-7 dissenting). 4. Exploration of SCP-7482-B is **suspended indefinitely**. All SCP-7482-A instances are to be sealed. No further entries authorized. **— Senior Archivist K. Velez, Department of Uncontained History**
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates exceptional adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving a complex narrative about cyclical civilizations and institutional memory. The author successfully captures the distinctive voice of SCP documentation - dry, clinical, yet increasingly unsettling as revelations unfold. The piece excels in its structural complexity, layering multiple narrative threads through recovered documents, exploration logs, and incident reports. The concept of the Foundation being merely the latest iteration of an ancient containment organization is genuinely creative and philosophically disturbing. The temporal paradoxes and identity questions (particularly around Dr. Vaughn and O5-14's simultaneous death and life) create genuine cognitive dissonance that enhances the horror. The exploration log section provides the most dynamic writing, with the backwards-retreating entities being a particularly memorable image. The dialogue feels authentic to military/scientific personnel, though it's limited. The gradual revelation structure builds tension effectively, with each document excerpt adding layers to the mystery. However, the piece occasionally becomes dense with exposition, particularly in the technical descriptions of the archive's architecture. Some sections read more like a technical manual than narrative fiction. The ending, while appropriately dark, feels somewhat rushed given the complexity of the setup. The characterization is necessarily limited by the SCP format, but what exists feels authentic. The institutional paranoia and the suggestion that the O5 Council has been complicit in covering up their own cyclical nature adds psychological depth. The imagery of the impossible archive, the hazmat-suited entities, and the temporal displacement creates a genuinely unsettling atmosphere. The piece maintains internal consistency despite its complex temporal elements, and the various plot threads interconnect logically. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The heat on Hain-Dhara did not fall; it rose, seeping up through the basalt paving stones into the soles of boots designed for ship-deck cold. Elara Vane pulled the collar of her Insulator Cloak higher. It was standard Corps issue: silver-weave, temperature-regulating, weighted at the hem to hang perfectly still in zero-g. Here, in the open-air market of Kethra, it hung like a shroud. She had left the reception at the Governor’s Spire through the service hatch, descending three levels of maintenance ladder to the city’s actual floor. Protocol demanded an escort, a briefing packet, a secure channel. Elara had left her comm badge on the dresser. The market smelled of salt, ozone, and something floral and rotting—*kesh-fruit*, the briefing called it, a staple carbohydrate. The briefing called many things staples. It called the people *variants*. They were not variants. Not here. A woman passed Elara, moving with a loose, hip-swaying gait that belonged to a gravity well. She wore a harness of woven fiber, bare-chested, her skin a deep, lustrous charcoal—melanin pushed to its evolutionary limit by a sun that spat hard UV. Her eyes were large, liquid, protected by a nictitating membrane that flicked sideways as she assessed the offworlder. Gills, faint and pink, fluttered at her neck as she breathed the heavy, oxygen-rich air. A *Littoral*, the briefing said. *Amphibious adaptation. Limited land range.* She carried a basket of translucent eels on her hip, and a child clung to her back, wrapped in a sling, its skin a lighter grey, its gills still sealed against the air. The woman didn’t stare at the cloak. She stared at Elara’s face—pale, dry, eyes hidden behind standard-issue polarizing lenses. The woman’s lips peeled back, revealing teeth filed to serrated points. A threat display? A greeting? The briefing had no entry for *smile*. Elara lowered her lenses. The woman’s expression softened. She clicked her tongue, a sound like stones striking underwater, and touched two fingers to her own sternum, then extended them to Elara. *I see you.* Elara mirrored the gesture, her gloved fingers clumsy against the heavy silk. *I see you.* The woman bared her teeth again—definitely a smile—and melted back into the current of bodies. Elara walked deeper. The architecture here was grown, not built: vast, ribbed shells of calcified secretions, honeycombed with apertures. *Coral-kin*, the briefing labeled them. *Sessile caste. Low mobility. High cognitive specialization for systems management.* She saw no castes. She saw a man—tall, elongated, his limbs jointed with an extra articulation, skin pale as milk-glass—arguing animatedly with a stocky, barrel-chested woman whose skin held the greenish tint of chloroplast symbiosis. They were haggling over a bundle of fiber-optic cable. The *Sylvestris* and the *Photosyn* were sharing a pipe of smoked lichen, passing it back and forth with easy intimacy. The briefing insisted their metabolic needs made cohabitation impossible. The briefing insisted the colony was a powder keg of resource competition, segregated by biology. The briefing was a lie written by people who had never smelled the air. She found a stall selling water. Not ration-packs. Water. In ceramic cups. The vendor was a *High-Grav*—dense-boned, squat, arms like tree roots. He didn't ask for credits. He watched her drink, the cool liquid shocking her dehydrated throat. "First drop?" he asked. His voice was a rumble, subsonic harmonics vibrating in Elara’s chest. "First drop," she admitted. "Tastes of iron and algae," he said. "Tastes like home. You’ll miss it when you go back to the clean dark." "I'm not staying," she said. He shrugged, a geological movement. "None of you do. But you carry the weight anyway." He tapped her cloak. "That thing. It keeps the dark in. Keeps the world out." "It regulates," she said, defensive. "Regulates you into a ghost," he countered. "Take it off. The sun won't eat you. Not today." She looked at the silver fabric. It was her uniform. Her shield. She unclasped the magnetic seals. The air hit her skin—wet, heavy, smelling of life. It was obscene. It was baptism. She folded the cloak over her arm, feeling suddenly naked, her Corps jumpsuit thin and grey against the riot of color and flesh around her. A breeze stirred the market, carrying pollen and spores. She breathed it in. Her lungs burned, sweet and sharp. *** The reprimand waited in her quarters, projected cold and blue from the comm unit on the wall. *"Envoy Vane. Your biometrics indicate unauthorized egress. Your tracker was disabled. Article 14, Section 3: Diplomatic personnel remain in secure zones pending threat assessment. Explain."* The voice was Admiralty Standard, flat and sexless. The voice of the Center, speaking from light-years away. Elara sat on the edge of the bunk, the cloak draped over the chair. Her skin still prickled with the market’s heat. "Threat assessment is incomplete, Command. The briefing data is flawed." *"The briefing is compiled from thirty years of orbital telemetry and reported incidents. Your observation window was forty-seven minutes. Reinstate tracker. Await Minister Kaelen."* The channel cut. She reactivated the tracker. The red light blinked on her wrist: *MONITORED.* She didn't have long to wait. The door chimed. Not a knock. A chime. Minister Kaelen entered without waiting for acknowledgment. He was a small man, soft in the way of lifelong administrators, dressed in the charcoal tunic of the Colonial Ministry. His hands were manicured, folded before him. He wore no cloak. He wore no weapon. He carried the absolute authority of the Center’s indifference. "Envoy Vane," he said. His voice was cultured, gentle. "The Admiralty is... exercised. A diplomatic incident on Day One. Walking the Lower Market. Unescorted. Unshielded." "The Lower Market is the city, Minister," Elara said. She stood, but did not salute. "The Spire is the anomaly." Kaelen smiled. It did not reach his eyes, which were the pale, watery blue of someone who had never seen a horizon uncurved by a viewport. "A poet. The Corps sends me a poet. I was promised a negotiator." "I negotiate with reality, sir. The briefings you provided negotiate with fantasy." "Fantasy keeps the peace," Kaelen said, drifting toward the viewport. He looked out at the grown city, the ribbed shells glowing with bioluminescence as the twin suns set. "Thirty years ago, the *Littoral* enclave blockaded the desalination plants. The *High-Grav* miners sabotaged the mag-lev. The *Photosyn* communes poisoned the hydroponics. Three thousand dead. We call it the Schism War. You call it a market." "I call it a Tuesday," Elara said. "They were sharing a pipe, Minister. The *Sylvestris* and the *Photosyn*. Trading cable. Breathing the same air." "Anomalies. Exceptions that prove the rule. The rule is biology. The rule is that the *Littoral* cannot survive the dry season without the *High-Grav* pumps, and the *High-Grav* cannot survive the wet season without the *Littoral* filtration. They hate the dependency. They hate each other. My job—our job—is to manage the hate so it doesn't become slaughter." "By lying to them?" Elara stepped closer. "By telling them they are separate species who require a distant Empire to arbitrate their existence?" "I tell them what they need to hear to maintain the treaty," Kaelen said, turning. The gentleness vanished, replaced by a scalpel’s edge. "And you, Envoy? What do you tell them? That you walked among them for an hour, shed your cloak, and now you *understand*? That is the most dangerous lie of all. The Le Guin Protocol—" "Don't invoke the Protocol," Elara snapped. "The Protocol demands *observation without interference*. I interfered the moment I landed. We all do. The question is whether we interfere to preserve the Empire’s map, or the territory." Kaelen laughed, a dry, papery sound. "The territory. How quaint. There is no territory, Envoy. There is only the map. The Empire *is* the map. Without the Center, this colony is a collection of incompatible biological niches fighting over water and air. With the Center, it is a Unified Protectorate. A single line on a chart. That is the only unity that matters." "And the people?" "The people are the terrain," Kaelen said. "Terrain is managed. It is not... consulted." He stepped into her personal space. He smelled of ozone and recycled air. The smell of the Center. "Here is your test, Envoy Vane. The Admiralty wants a report. They want to know if the 'tensions' require a garrison battalion or a trade envoy. They want a binary. Give them a binary. Tell them the subspecies are integrating. Recommend a trade mission. It costs nothing. It validates the Center’s benevolence. It keeps the map clean." "And if they aren't integrating?" Elara asked, her voice low. "If the market is a pause, not a peace? If the dependency is a noose?" "Then you recommend the battalion," Kaelen said. "But you won't. Because you took off your cloak. Because you drank the water. Because you want to believe in the Tuesday. And that, Envoy, is why you are here. Not to see. But to *want*." He turned to leave, then paused at the door. "Retrieve your cloak. The nights here drop to freezing. The *Littoral* retreat to the sumps. The *High-Grav* seal their warrens. The *Photosyn* go dormant. The market closes. The city becomes what the map says it is: a collection of sealed boxes." He left. The door sealed with a pneumatic hiss. Elara stood alone in the sudden silence of the quarters. The recycler hummed. The light panels mimicked a standard diurnal cycle. She walked to the chair. She picked up the silver cloak. It was heavy. It smelled of ship-air, of sterility, of the Center. She held it for a long time, feeling the weight of the map in her hands. Outside, the bioluminescence of the grown city pulsed, a slow, green heartbeat against the dark. Somewhere in the sumps, a gill-flutter clicked. Somewhere in the warrens, a dense bone knocked on a dense door. Elara unclasped the magnetic seals of her jumpsuit at the neck. She let the cool night air touch her throat. She draped the cloak over the chair back, silver on grey. "Computer," she said. "Open the balcony doors. And log a personal addendum to the daily report. Priority Alpha." *"Acknowledged. Recording."* "Tell the Admiralty the map is wrong," she said, stepping out onto the balcony, into the wet, heavy, unbearable dark. "Tell them the territory is breathing. And tell Minister Kaelen... tell him I passed his test. I still want to believe in Tuesday. But I'm bringing a battalion anyway. Just in case the want is wrong." She leaned on the rail, watching the city sleep in its separate skins, connected only by the roots they refused to acknowledge, and the pipes they couldn't live without. *"Addendum logged. Transmitting to Command."* The red light on her wrist blinked steady. *MONITORED.* Elara Vane closed her eyes, and listened to the sound of a world that refused to stay drawn.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's literary style and thematic preoccupations. The author successfully captures Le Guin's anthropological approach to science fiction, her interest in cultural relativism, and her elegant, measured prose style. The worldbuilding is particularly strong, presenting a believable future where human subspecies have evolved distinct biological adaptations while maintaining recognizable humanity. The narrative structure effectively follows the prompt requirements, moving from the envoy's unauthorized exploration through the political confrontation with Minister Kaelen. The protagonist Elara Vane is well-developed, showing genuine curiosity and moral complexity rather than simple rebelliousness. Her transformation from protocol-following diplomat to someone willing to challenge the system feels earned through her direct experiences in the market. The dialogue between Elara and Minister Kaelen is the story's strongest element, presenting two competing worldviews with nuance. Kaelen is not a simple antagonist but a pragmatist with his own logic, making the conflict more intellectually engaging. His test of Elara's character through philosophical challenge rather than crude manipulation feels authentic to Le Guin's approach to political complexity. The prose maintains Le Guin's characteristic restraint while still being evocative. Descriptions like "The heat on Hain-Dhara did not fall; it rose" and "Terrain is managed. It is not... consulted" capture her voice effectively. The biological details of the subspecies are creative and scientifically plausible without becoming overly technical. The ending strikes an appropriate balance between hope and realism. Elara's decision to recommend both diplomatic engagement and military backup reflects the story's central theme about the complexity of colonial relationships and the inadequacy of simple solutions. This avoids both naive optimism and cynical darkness. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Le Guin pastiche becomes slightly self-conscious, and a few descriptions that edge toward purple prose. The pacing is generally strong, though the market sequence could have been slightly tighter. Overall, this is a highly accomplished piece that successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while creating an engaging standalone narrative. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 73.7
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The centrifuge whined, a sound like a dying mosquito amplified inside a tin can. Kaelen didn't flinch. He knew the exact harmonic frequency where the 3D-printed rotor brackets resonated, and he knew the duct tape wrapping the motor housing would hold for another forty seconds. Thirty-nine. Thirty-eight. He watched the separation through the scratched polycarbonate lid. Red cells packing tight at the bottom. Buffy coat a thin, dirty line in the middle. Plasma, straw-yellow and precious, rising to the top. "Stable," he muttered, his voice rasping against the dry air of the shipping container lab. "Hold the line." The timer beeped. He killed the power, the whine descending into a death rattle. He extracted the tubes with tweezers fashioned from a snapped antenna and a binder clip, transferring the plasma into a row of **empty Helix Dynamics canisters**. The blue hexagonal logo was scratched off most of them, but the molded serial numbers on the base remained: *HD-7700 Series. Single-Use Lysate Buffer. Property of Helix Dynamics Global. Unauthorized Refill Voids Genetic Warranty.* Kaelen liked the irony. The warranty had expired when the grid went down. The company had expired when the shareholders realized they’d eaten their own seed corn. The canisters, however, were borosilicate grade, rated for -196°C and autoclavable. Best reagent bottles in the Wastes. He had three hundred of them stacked in crates behind the water reclamation unit, looted from a distribution hub outside what used to be Denver. He pipetted the plasma into a canister marked with a grease-pencil 'X'. *Fraction 4. High IgG. Low protease.* His left hand tremored as he set the pipette down. A fine, high-frequency vibration in the fingers. The *upside* of the CRISPR-Cas12a cocktail he’d brewed last month to clear the fungal pneumonia eating his lungs. The *toll* was a peripheral neuropathy that made fine motor work a gamble. The *upside* was he could smell the difference between *Pseudomonas* and *Bacillus* contamination from three meters away. His olfactory bulb had rewired itself to express a variant of the OR5A1 receptor, tuned to geosmin and 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. He smelled dirt and popcorn where others smelled only rot. "Trade-off," he whispered, massaging his wrist. "Everything’s a trade-off." The airlock hissed. Positive pressure failed, sucking in a gust of hot, dust-smelling air. Kaelen didn't reach for the rifle mounted by the door. He reached for the UV wand, waving it over the entry vector. A figure stepped in, backlit by the harsh noon sun. Heavy boots. A duster coat patched with Kevlar scraps. A respirator mask with custom filters—pink charcoal, rated for viral load and spore bloom. "Smells like popcorn in here," the figure said, voice synthesized through the mask’s vox-unit. "Burnt popcorn." "Geosmin," Kaelen corrected, capping the 'X' canister. "Means the *Streptomyces* in the soil bed are sporulating. Means my antibiotics are working. You're late, Vance." Vance shrugged, dropping a heavy pelican case onto the stainless steel prep table (a repurposed autopsy gurney). "Roads washed out at the Arkansas crossing. Had to detour through the Spore Fields. Lost a tire to a root-knot the size of a fist." "Payment's in the case?" "Half now. Half on delivery. Standard contract." Vance unclipped the case. Inside, nestled in foam cutouts, sat two objects. A sealed, nitrogen-flushed vial containing a desiccated leaf fragment—*Zea mays*, pre-Collapse, heirloom genotype. And a data drive, scarred by impact fractures. Kaelen picked up the vial. The glass was Helix Dynamics. *HD-9900. Germplasm Archive. Viability Guarantee: 1 Generation.* The Obsolescence Clause. The masterstroke of late-stage biocapitalism. Helix hadn't just sold seeds; they sold *time*. The telomeres in the chloroplast genomes were engineered with a synthetic intron splice site that failed catastrophically during meiosis I. The F1 generation grew tall, sweet, nutrient-dense. The F2 seeds germinated into chimeric horrors—roots growing from leaves, photosynthesis pathways running in reverse, cyanide precursors accumulating in the kernels. Farmers had to buy fresh F1 stock every season. Perpetual subscription to life. Until the servers hosting the epigenetic keys went dark. Until the seed banks froze solid or cooked in their own backup generators. Now, the world ate algae paste and insect flour, while the last viable F1 kernels were worth more than gold. "Golden Harvest 9," Kaelen said, reading the faded barcode on the vial. "High lysine. Drought tolerant. *Terminator gene active*." "Active," Vance confirmed. "We need the terminator excised. We need an F2 that breeds true. We need it in six weeks. Planting window closes at the solstice." "Six weeks," Kaelen laughed, a dry hack. "You want me to rewrite the fundamental reproductive biology of a monocot in six weeks? With a helicase that degrades if I look at it wrong? The helicase *I* synthesized in a pressure cooker because the thermocycler’s Peltier block died three days ago?" "The settlement at New Canaan has three hundred mouths," Vance said, the vox stripping the empathy from the words. "They have the land. They have the water. They don't have the code. You're the only splicer in the sector with a functioning—mostly functioning—long-read sequencer. The contract says: *Viable F2 Germline. Heritable. Stable.* Price is non-negotiable." Kaelen set the vial down. He looked at his trembling left hand. Then at the jury-rigged sequencer—a MinION flow cell clamped into a 3D-printed housing, fed by a peristaltic pump salvaged from a dialysis machine, reading DNA strands through a nanopore the size of a virus. The laptop driving it ran a stripped Linux kernel, cooled by a loop of glycol tapped from the container’s AC unit. "Sequencing the terminator locus is easy," Kaelen said. "Excising it is easy. *Stabilizing the genome afterwards* is the bitch. Helix didn't just put a kill switch in the telomeres. They peppered the genome with synthetic lethals. Cryptic splice sites. Poison exons. You remove the terminator, the plant expresses a latent ribosome-inactivating protein in the pollen. Sterility by design. Redundancy upon redundancy." "I read the white papers," Vance said. "You published the workaround for the *Bt*-toxin feedback loop in the Denver settlement's kale crop. You fixed the ribosomal frameshift." "That was a frameshift. A typo. This is a minefield." Kaelen pulled up a stool. "I need the epigenome. The methylation patterns. The helicase loader proteins. The vial only gives me the naked DNA. If I don't have the maternal imprinting factors, the endosperm fails. The seed aborts at day twelve." "The drive has the methylome," Vance said. "Lifted from a Helix cold storage server in '32. Before the purge. It’s raw nanopore signal. Basecalled, but raw." Kaelen plugged the drive in. The laptop fan screamed. Lines of code scrolled—fast5 files, thousands of them. He felt the familiar spike of adrenaline, sharp and clean, clearing the neuropathy fog. *Focus.* The mod in his adrenal medulla (a lentiviral vector he’d cooked up to survive a crush injury three years back) dumped norepinephrine on command. The cost: he hadn't slept more than ninety minutes at a stretch since 2038. The benefit: he could hold a 50kb genome assembly in working memory like a chess master. "Okay," Kaelen breathed. "Okay. The methylome is here. CpG islands on Chromosome 4 and 9. The imprinting control regions... they're methylated. Good. Maternal allele silenced. We can work with this." He stood up, moving to the tissue culture hood. A laminar flow cabinet built from a HEPA filter meant for a cleanroom fab, a box fan, and a sheet of acrylic. Inside, on agar plates dyed green with BAP medium, sat the *real* work. Not corn. *Arabidopsis thaliana*. Thale cress. The lab rat of the plant world. Generation 47 of his own line. *Kaelen-47 Express*. He popped the lid of a plate. The seedlings were wrong. Glowing faintly, bioluminescent reporters (lux operon from *Vibrio fischeri*) tied to the *WUSCHEL* promoter—meristem activity. But the leaves were serrated like saw blades, thickened, waxy. The roots, visible through the clear agar, were purple—anthocyanin overproduction, a stress marker he’d linked to the heat-shock promoter. He peeled a leaf from a glowing mutant. *Crunch.* Crisp. High cellulose. "Eat your vegetables, Kaelen," he whispered. He chewed the leaf. Bitter, metallic. The anthocyanins hit his modified tongue—bitter receptors upregulated, sweet receptors knocked out. *Discipline.* He swallowed. The purple pigment, a customized flavonoid pathway, would hit his bloodstream in twenty minutes. Vasodilation. Neuroprotection. A temporary patch for the tremor. The toll: his urine would stain the porcelain blue for two days. The upside: his hands would stop shaking long enough to inject the CRISPR ribonucleoprotein complexes into the corn embryogenic callus. "Vance," Kaelen said, wiping green sap from his lips. "Get the incubator ready. The big one. The one with the CO2 tank. I need callus induction media. 2,4-D. Kinetin. Silver nitrate. And find me a Helix canister—clean one—label it 'RNP Complex - Do Not Drink.'" Vance nodded, already moving to the shelving unit. "Six weeks?" "Five," Kaelen said, stripping off his nitrile gloves, the tremor already fading as the flavonoid rush hit his cerebellum. "Five weeks to F1 seed. One more to verify F2 germination. You get your true-breeding corn. I get..." He glanced at the stack of blue canisters, then at the glowing *Arabidopsis*. He tapped his temple. "I get to keep the lights on. And maybe, if the frameshift holds in the meristem... I get a crop that doesn't taste like ash." He picked up the pipette. The tremor was gone. The world resolved into base pairs. A, T, C, G. The only currency that mattered. "Let's break the warranty," Kaelen said, and plunged the tip into the vial of dead gold.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk piece demonstrates strong technical writing and worldbuilding, creating a convincing post-apocalyptic laboratory setting where genetic engineering has collapsed due to built-in obsolescence. The author shows impressive knowledge of molecular biology, seamlessly integrating real scientific terminology (CRISPR-Cas12a, nanopore sequencing, methylation patterns) with plausible future technology. The protagonist Kaelen is well-developed through his actions and internal monologue. His physical modifications and their trade-offs (enhanced smell but tremors, better focus but insomnia) create compelling character depth. The writing effectively shows his expertise and desperation without excessive exposition. His relationship with his own body as both laboratory and subject adds psychological complexity. The prose is generally strong, with vivid sensory details and technical precision that serves the genre well. The opening centrifuge sequence immediately establishes both setting and character competence. Scientific jargon is deployed naturally rather than feeling forced or show-offy. However, the piece suffers from some pacing issues. The middle section becomes dense with technical exposition that, while accurate, slows narrative momentum. Some descriptions veer toward purple prose ("death rattle," "ate their own seed corn") though this generally serves the dystopian atmosphere. The dialogue between Kaelen and Vance functions adequately but lacks distinctive voice - both characters speak in similar technical, clipped tones. Vance particularly feels underdeveloped, serving mainly as exposition delivery. The black market contract plot provides clear stakes and urgency, though the resolution feels somewhat predictable - the brilliant loner scientist accepting the impossible challenge. The ending's confidence ("Let's break the warranty") feels earned given Kaelen's established expertise, but the transformation from reluctance to determination happens quite rapidly. The worldbuilding excels, particularly the corporate genetic engineering backstory and the practical details of jury-rigged equipment. The Helix Dynamics canisters and warranty language effectively illustrate how capitalism commodified life itself. Overall, this is competent genre fiction with strong technical foundations and atmospheric writing, though it doesn't transcend familiar post-apocalyptic scientist tropes.
